speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF LATE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find it more difficult than usual to find words adequately to express the grief that I know we all feel at the passing of our Governor General. That difficulty for me is increased by the recollection of our close personal friendship over so many years.
Since his death on Sunday morning messages have been coming in from the great in the world and from plain citizens in Canada, all testifying, high and low alike, to the affection that was felt for him by everyone. Among the first messages to arrive was one from Her Majesty the Queen, whose servant and representative in Canada he was. This message, which has already been made public, read:
My husband and I are so deeply distressed to hear the tragic news of the Governor General's death. We send our deepest sympathy to you and the Canadian people and the Canadian government in the loss of this most distinguished Canadian.
He was indeed, Mr. Speaker, a distinguished Canadian and his whole life is a record of that distinction; a record of his service to Canada, a record of willing acceptance in peace and in war of every duty he was asked to perform or, perhaps I should put it, of every duty that he asked to be permitted to perform.
As we know, Mr. Speaker, General Vanier was trained for the bar to which he was called in 1911. He answered the call to arms shortly afterwards and served for three years in France as a gallant officer of a gallant regiment whose traditions he helped to create and maintain. The Distinguished Service Order, the Military Cross and bar and the Legion of Honour attest to his courage. His wounds attest to his sacrifices. After the war he returned to civilian life for a very short time, then again took up a military career, as a member of the permanent forces.
During the years he was in the army there was a steady promotion to new responsibilities until in 1928, I think it was, he was asked to be the Canadian military representative on the disarmament commission of the League of Nations at Geneva. At that time he acquired the interest in diplomacy and international affairs and in peace keeping which he retained throughout his life and which was recognized a few years later, in 1931, by the government of the day when he was made the secretary of the office of the high commissioner in London. It was at that time that our official and family association began, Mr. Speaker, which was broken only by his death.
After serving at Canada House in London, General Vanier was made Canadian minister to France. After the outbreak of war and the collapse of France in 1940 he returned after a series of adventures to London, where I had the privilege of meeting him and Madame Vanier on their return. Although he had been going through some pretty difficult and dangerous moments he had that calm imperturbability and good humour that always characterized him in any difficulty. During the war he went to Algiers, where he was the Canadian representative to the Free French government headed by General de Gaulle and established a relationship and friendship with General de Gaulle which has persisted to the present. Then after the liberation he went back to Paris as Canadian ambassador, where he and his wife became outstanding members of the diplomatic corps.
On his retirement from the diplomatic service he might well have looked forward to some years of peace and tranquility, but when he was asked by the prime minister of the day, now the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, to be Governor General he naturally accepted it as a call to duty. When his normal term of office ended and I as Prime Minister asked him to stay on, he agreed to do that at my request as long as his health permitted. That was permitted by his health until last week.
As you know, he had an operation last autumn, but he was recovering well from it except for his heart. I went to see him at Rideau Hall last Wednesday, after he had

Tributes to Late Georges Philias Vanier been examined by specialists, in order to discuss with him whether his health would permit him to take on the very heavy duties of Governor General during our centennial year. We agreed to meet again on Friday, and at that time he indicated that he felt he would not likely be able to continue in office.
On Friday afternoon he made his last appearance before a group, when he talked to students of the University of Montreal very eloquently and impressively on a subject so dear to his heart, namely Canadian unity and the part which French speaking Canadians can play in the development of this country. Then, as we have learned, he spent Saturday evening indulging in a favourite pastime, watching the hockey game on television, and he enjoyed the victory of his favourite team. On Sunday morning this good and faithful servant passed away peacefully and quietly, without pain and with the spiritual solace of the last rites of his church.
His public career, as we know, was marked with distinction and wisdom in everything he undertook and with a broad understanding of Canada and its problems, coupled with faith and confidence in our ability as a people to solve those problems. He had a passionate belief in this country, in its unity, in its destiny of true greatness based on enduring values and patriotic ideals which should be shared by all its citizens. He made Canada and its unity his own crusade, in every word he uttered, in every visit he made and on every occasion that he honoured with his presence.
His French ancestors were among the very first settlers in Canada. He was very proud of that ancestry, but prouder still, I think, of the Canada of today. With roots so deep in our soil, he also saw far into the future and gave his all to make it a good future for the country he loved.
All his life he maintained that keen and expert interest in defence matters that befitted such a distinguished soldier and the commander in chief of the armed forces. He was always particularly interested in the welfare of the veterans. He was grand patron and honorary life member of the Canadian Legion, and he was the comrade of every legionnaire and every veteran.
As a man he had the dignity of the true patrician and the modesty and simplicity of the true gentleman. He had the calm security and inner strength that come from a deep belief in the Christian faith. His religion

DEBATES	March 6, 1967
meant very much to him indeed. He was a devout man without being sanctimonious. He was a serious man but with a delicious sense of humour. He was a man of high quality without being stuffy or superior. Indeed, I believe our Governor General embodied in his own person and in his own life and achievements all that is best in Canadians and all that we hope for our country.
When General Vanier was installed as Governor General on April 15, 1959, he said this:
Each one of us, in his own way and place, however humble, must play his part towards the fulfilment of our national destiny. To realize how mighty this destiny will be let us lift our eyes beyond the horizon of our time. In our march forward in material happiness, let us not neglect the spiritual threads in the weaving of our lives. If Canada is to attain the greatness worthy of it, each of us must say "I ask only to serve".
His request was granted. No Canadian has ever served more abundantly, more unselfishly or more gallantly.
We also think at this time of Madame Vanier, a very gracious, generous and, indeed, wonderful person who has earned and will retain her own place in the esteem and affection of the Canadian people. She was the perfect partner for her husband over the years; to his strength and his character she added her own superlative qualities of grace, kindliness and warmth. To Madame Vanier and to the children, who are following the family tradition of service, I am sure we all in this house would wish to send our deep and heartfelt sympathy. I know they are all getting comfort and support in this dark time from a faith which has given them the peace which passes all human understanding. To this spiritual peace is added the solace which comes from pride in the life of one dear to them, a life which had nothing in it of littleness or meanness, and everything that makes for a happy memory.
Mr. Speaker, when I saw the Governor General on Friday evening and he indicated to me that he did not think it would be possible for him to carry on, I said I hoped we could find some way of maintaining his association with our centennial year even if he did leave Rideau Hall. Then I made an observation which was picked, as it were, out of the air. I said "What we should do is give you a position which would in no way tax your strength but which would maintain your association with Canada in this centennial year; and perhaps I will ask you to go down to Quebec and take up residence there, at least for 1967, as Keeper of the Citadel."
March 6, 1967	COMMONS
He smiled at the idea of becoming a keeper. Indeed, it would have been a small honour for a man who throughout his life was the keeper of the citadel of truth and faith and honour.

subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF LATE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, His Excellency General Vanier, Governor General of Canada, is dead. He departed very peacefully from this life on earth for the other in which he believed so deeply. His death does not seem like a break or an end but rather an expected transition which did not disturb the continuous and coherent course of his life.
Those who had the privilege to talk with the Governor General in the last months before his death could not help but notice the elevation of his thoughts and feelings. The breath of life which still kept him here revealed to us, without his being aware of it, the spiritual level which he had reached and which left human values far behind. Not that he had lost all interest in our problems. On the contrary, a few weeks ago in a private conversation, I had the honour of discussing with him the great problems which concern our world. I was amazed at the keen interest he took in the future of this country, to understanding between groups, to the brotherhood of men. From his lofty position, in spite of his wavering health, he was present and active to the end.
His Excellency General Vanier was the first French speaking Canadian to occupy the position of Governor General of Canada since Confederation. This event marks an important stage in the evolution of this country, because his appointment was not merely an act of condescension towards French Canadians. During his military and diplomatic careers, he was the embodiment of our people's aspirations, as well as the human symbol of our common ideal.
I hope the life of this great man who has just passed away will serve as an example for all those who believe in justice, peace and brotherhood.
All French Canadians, I am sure, wish the family of His Excellency to accept their heartfelt sympathy.
In conclusion Mr. Speaker I shall simply quote these few lines of verse by Charles Peguy:

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF LATE GOVERNOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, how little any of us thought when we adjourned on Friday that we would meet today under the tragic circumstance of the loss of our Governor General.
It is my sad duty this afternoon, in the unavoidable absence of the leader of Her Majesty's loyal opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), to add to the tribute paid to General Vanier by the Prime Minister an expression of the sorrow that lies heavily at this time on the hearts of my colleagues here, and on their behalf to pay our heartfelt respects to the memory of a very great Canadian. As perhaps no other governor general in our history he was known and loved by every member of this house, and to an amazing extent by the millions of Canadians whom we have the honour to represent here.
1 speak, too, of the sympathy we all feel for the gracious lady who was so often our hostess at Rideau Hall, whose charm and poise have so often been the chief ornament of this parliament in the other place, and whose so sudden bereavement cries out for the utmost of our sympathy, understanding and appreciation of the great loss that has come to her, to her sons and daughters, as well as to us and all Canadians.
Today we pay our profoundest respects not only to his memory as the representative of the Queen of Canada and head of the Commonwealth but also to his memory as a man, one would almost say the ideal man, and certainly one who set a standard and example of Canadian manhood which we would hope to see every one of our fellow citizens, young or old, emulate.
The word that will be linked over and over again with his career and character will be "gentleman". It is, perhaps, an old fashioned word. No one who knew him will say that he was in the ordinary sense old fashioned, but he did practise, as none other I have known, the old fashioned virtues of courtesy, kindness and consideration for his fellow men
13756	COMMONS
Tributes to Late Georges Philias Vanier whatever their station in life, whatever their creed or colour.
"A Christian," said Robert Louis Stevenson, "is God Almighty's gentleman." General Vanier was that kind of gentleman. During his term of office he gave a new dimension to the term Canadian. He was the first French Canadian since the Marquis de Vaudreuil to hold the post of governor general. Representing a different crown there was, nevertheless, a dedication and devotion unsurpassed.
He acted at all times with a largeness of view extending from the Atlantic to the Pacific encompassing the many shades and varieties of opinion, race and creed which make up the greatness of this nation. He was a great Canadian. In the tradition of Macdonald and Laurier he was beloved by Canadians. His name will live in the annals of the nation as one personifying in his conduct and his beliefs a type of Canadianism which all can follow regardless of origin.
This was a man whose vision of confederation was such that it embodied a living reality. He saw confederation as a rich stream of commonly shared experience and belief springing from two main cultural sources, widened, deepened and strengthened by the later infusions from other groups. He saw nothing contradictory in the flowing together of many cultures, all tending toward the same objective-a greater, finer and stronger Canada.
Surely we can all pay to his memory the tribute of our support of this powerful thesis, on the acceptance of which depends the future strength of this nation. Some of the things he said in his high office, with all the dignity and prestige of his personal and public stature will be remembered so long as there is a Canada. He stressed what is good, what is creative, and what is strong in our history and being. In his message on January 1, 1967 appear these thoughts:
-let us remember and cherish that which is creative in our history-if we imagine that we can now go our separate ways within our country; if we think that selfish interests can now take precedence over the national good; if we exaggerate our differences or revel in contention; if we do any of these things, we will promote our own destruction-
His last formal message to Canada in that address was this:
The resolution which the Canadian nation must now propose for 1967 and for the century to come, is the unity of our country.

DEBATES	March 6, 1967
Mr. Speaker, as a member of this house and speaking on behalf of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, I endorse those words and put them forward as a goal toward which we must all strive. Their adoption is the greatest tribute we at this stage can pay to a great man who has passed from our midst.
A soldier of the Queen to the last breath; a patriot, statesman, devoted Canadian; an ornament to his province, his people and his nation; let us all unite in saluting a Canadian whose greatness we shall not soon see again.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the death of General Georges P. Vanier plunges all Canadians into deep mourning, and French Canadians are particularly grieved.
The dignity with which this great Canadian discharged his military and diplomatic duties, as well as those of Governor General, has gained French Canadians much admiration and respect on the part of all Canadians. General Vanier was the true image of French Canada, namely respect for tradition and order. He was also proud of the part he had been given to play in history.
When he became the Queen's representative, General Vanier was succeeding another great Canadian, His Excellency the Right Hon. Vincent Massey, who was the first Canadian ever to hold such high office.
General Vanier's stay at Rideau Hall has shown that the two founding peoples of confederation have within their ranks men capable of serving their country with honour and attaining the highest position to which a Canadian can aspire.
The name of General Vanier will be inscribed in letters of gold in the history of Canada. His personal qualities, his wisdom and his courage will forever be a source of inspiration as well as legitimate pride to his compatriots.
General Vanier was not content to assume passively the role of representative of the crown. On the contrary. His inexhaustible optimism and dynamism inspired the life of the community. The Vanier Institute of the Family will stand as a lasting monument to his memory.
To Madame Vanier, so sorely tried, who contributed immeasurably to the affection we all felt for General Vanier, to the children and relatives of the illustrious deceased, I offer, on behalf of the French speaking Canadians, the condolences of a people who will always consider General Vanier as one of its noblest sons.

Mr. Speaker, in common with all Canadians, the members of the New Democratic Party are saddened and distressed at the passing of Governor General Georges P. Vanier, and we join most sincerely with those who have spoken in paying tribute to his memory.
Throughout the years we have had not only a profound respect and admiration for his public service but also a deep personal affection for him as a kind and warm hearted person. During his long term as Governor General he and Madame Vanier have broken through the trappings of their high office to endear themselves to us and to Canadians in every walk of life. His death at this time occasions a sense of personal loss as well as regret at the passing of an outstanding public figure.
The late Governor General was the personification of the dedicated public servant. In war and in peace he gave of himself unstintingly with modest courage and quiet determination. His heroism on the battlefield has added lustre to the already magnificent traditions of the famous Van Doos. His performance in a succession of overseas posts demonstrated his stature as a competent and effective diplomat.
But it was in the role of Governor General that he made his most lasting contribution to Canada. The grace and charm which His Excellency and Madame Vanier displayed won the hearts of the Canadian people. It was clear from the beginning that they loved the Canadian people and they were soon beloved by them in return. Personally what I shall cherish most in my memory of the late Governor General was his unfailing kindness to people in the every day walks of life. To me he will always be associated with the lines of Wordsworth:
That best portion of a good man's life,-
His little, nameless, unremembered acts
Of kindness and of love.
General Vanier was the first French speaking Canadian to occupy the high post of the Queen's representative in this country. He himself was the personification of the finest attributes and culture of the two races that laid the foundations of Canadian confederation. Few men have done more to promote a better understanding and mutual appreciation between French speaking and English speaking Canadians than the late Governor General. His New Year's message to the
23033-870a
Tributes to Late Georges Philias Vanier Canadian people was a plea for good will and forbearance in learning to live together in harmony. But it was more than that. It was a challenge to all Canadians to realize the potential enrichment that can come from a bicultural and bilingual society. If Canada is to survive as a viable nation it must produce more men of the calibre of Georges P. Vanier.
Example is often much more important than pronouncements, no matter how sincerely they are expressed. The greatest contribution of the Vaniers may well be the lasting effect of their personal lives. With clear insight they recognized that the family is the heart of a nation's life. The formation of the Vanier Institute of the Family could be the most lasting memorial to one who in addition to being a distinguished public servant was also a good man in the finest meaning of that word.
General Vanier's concern for the family as the well-spring of our national life was undoubtedly motivated by his own happy family life. His successful tenure of office as Governor General was enhanced by the devoted assistance of his gracious, charming and highly intelligent wife. Together they symbolized all that was best in Canadian life, and they displayed a genuine fondness for people which was reciprocated in increasing measure with the passing years.
Today we mourn the passing of one who was a great Canadian and a true friend. While we shall miss him we shall also be challenged by his example. Because he lived, Canada will be a better place and we shall all be better men and women. That is his tribute, and that will be his epitaph. All of us join in extending to Madame Vanier and the members of his family our deepest sympathy at the loss which they and we have sustained. Our sorrow is great, but it is lessened by the memory of a life lived to the full in dedicated service to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the whole country was saddened on learning of the death of His Excellency the Governor General, Mr. Georges P. Vanier. Every Canadian is moved and affected by the departure of this man who worked unceasingly to improve the lot of his fellow-men in all circumstances and everywhere he happened to be.

Mr. Speaker, his life activities, whether political, military, social or other, always reflected the great respect he had for his

I shall not try to give a life history of General Vanier. The Prime Minister has done so in a marvellous way. I am only sorry that I could not also have been a close personal friend of His Excellency. However, with all Canadians I feel I was his friend because his lifetime activities devoted to the welfare and benefit of the Canadian people could not but make one feel a close relationship with the greatness of this man. As a young member of parliament I feel it my duty to ask young Canadians today to look upon Georges P. Vanier as I do; as a model of a true, honest and sincere Canadian.

It is all the more of a privilege, Mr. Speaker, that General Vanier was among my ancestors in the province of Quebec.
His activities, his sense of justice, his regard for Canada, the tasks he accomplished over a period of almost three quarters of a century, always striving to promote national unity, understanding and peace, in short, the achievements of this valorous man should make him an idol of all Canadians, whatever their origins.
French Canada can be proud of having produced such a great man. His labours, his patience, his devotion cover a period of three quarters of a century and I appeal to all Canadians, young, middle-aged and advanced in years, to consider that here was a true Canadian who was devoted to the welfare of his country, respectful of its traditions and convictions, while respectful of those of others.

Mr. Speaker, to any Canadian of the future General Georges P. Vanier will be as he was to those who knew him in his lifetime, a man of honour, wisdom and understanding, a just man and a man of great distinction who always had that humbleness about him that when I as a fairly young Canadian heard him speak, reminded me of my father. I think to the Canadian people he was everyone's father.

To Mrs. Vanier, her children and family, we extend our deepest sympathy.

Mr. Speaker, the members of the Social Credit party wish to join in expressing our sorrow and deep sense of loss in the passing of our respected and beloved Governor General, Georges P. Vanier. General Vanier's distinguished and heroic military career, his outstanding service in the diplomatic service of our country, and the efficient and dedicated manner in which he fulfilled his responsibilities as the representative of Her Majesty the Queen have combined to assure him of a special place in the hearts of Canadians and in the history of this nation.
While fully recognizing the outstanding contribution made in these important fields of service there is another area in which his example and influence and that of Madame Vanier will long be remembered and appreciated, namely in emphasizing the importance of spiritual values and the development and maintenance of the family as the foundation and bulwark of the nation. Deeply religious, warm hearted and sincere, dedicated and courageous, Governor General Vanier, though dead, still speaks, challenging us all to thrust aside those things which divide and destroy and to press forward under God to build an even greater and better nation.
We join in extending to Madame Vanier and the members of the family our sincere sympathy and the assurance of our prayers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I raise this question because of the fact that it has already received attention in the press, and to give the Prime Minister an opportunity to explain a situation that has already caused a great deal of questioning. Did the Prime Minister, in his constitutional position relative to Her Majesty, ask for representation of Her Majesty at the funeral of His Excellency the late Governor General? Was there such communication with the government of the United Kingdom? I ask the question because I know the Prime Minister will wish to clarify it before it assumes the proportions that are apparently developing.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: REPRESENTATION AT FUNERAL OF LATE GOVERNOR GENERAL

I do not know, Mr. Speaker, whether it is a proper question at all, but it has been asked. I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that I had been in touch with the palace on this matter immediately after the death of the Governor General.
I regret to have to report on this at this time, but I point out that when the administrator was sworn in Her Majesty the Queen was then represented by the administrator. He has all the powers of the Governor
General, and he represented the Queen. I think that was the proper constitutional procedure. It was up to the British government, of course, to decide how they would be represented at the funeral, and they were represented.

Anticipating a question of this sort I made inquiries as to what Mr. Rockefeller had actually said. The information I have is as follows. The first question put to Mr. Rockefeller was "What about the Mercantile mess? Why don't you sell out?" Mr. Chairman, the rules of this house with regard to debate on a bill of this kind make it a little difficult to mix general remarks with specific remarks relating to the bill, in that I want to discuss the determination of monetary policy and the maintenance or creation of statutory secondary reserves.
There is not a great deal in the act other than general housekeeping matters. If one refers back to the 1953-54 amendments which revised the act, as contained in the 1952 revised statutes, one can see that there are not now many changes in the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act. However, I feel there should be some remarks of a general nature made at this time and with your indulgence, Mr. Chairman, I should like to address myself to these subjects. My colleagues may have considerably more to say when we reach the individual clauses of the bill.
I wish to deal primarily with some of the testimony of Mr. Rasminsky, governor of the Bank of Canada, which appears in the minutes of proceedings and evidence No. 19 dated October 31, 1966. I am sorry I was not able to be present at this particular meeting of the committee, but in any event there is reproduced in the minutes for the edification and instruction of hon. members a fairly extensive brief which was presented by the governor and on which he was questioned.
One point with which I agree, and which is one of the crucial points made by Mr. Rasminsky, is that there is nothing in the bill which diminishes the responsibility which the governor bears for the monetary policy being followed. Then as reported at page 990 of the report the governor went on to say:
So long as he occupies the position of governor the public is entitled to assume that the policy being followed carries his personal judgment. As the minister said in the second reading debate in the House of Commons, if the government of the day ever issued a directive to the governor to execute a monetary policy which he felt was contrary to the public interest, it may be taken for granted that he would resign rather than accept such a responsibility.
I find some difficulty in the provision of the bill which, shall we say, statutorily enshrines this difference of opinion and which would put it beyond the pale of a reconsideration of
Bank of Canada Act
position either by the government or the governor so they could arrive at some consensus or at some variation. I want to discuss this further when we get to the appropriate clause, which is the proposed section 14, being clause 6 of this bill; but it seems to me that these differences of opinion have to be underlined by a written directive from the Minister of Finance, after consultation with the governor in council, to the governor of the Bank of Canada instructing him to follow a certain policy, which should be published in the Canada Gazette.
I think it would be beyond the pale that this should ever arise, Mr. Chairman. I just cannot conceive of any governor remaining in his position if he had to be subjected to this type of treatment. It might be that the government is now thinking that this would be an additional weapon with which to beat a governor-and I am referring to a recalcitrant governor-into submission. There is no doubt that monetary policy is the responsibility of the government.

Oh, no. The minister may want to play around with this, but he has had experience with the esteemed gentleman who was involved in this connection, and I am sure he would realize that if that man occupied his former position today there would be a great deal of difficulty. The minister would have to deal not only with the hon. member for Davenport but also with a governor of the Bank of Canada who at one time was making rather extraordinarily freelance speeches.
Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I found his behaviour at the time completely incomprehensible, and since then I have at times found his behaviour equally incomprehensible. However, I realize that the minister is trying to get some form of statutory power into the bill in order to deal with a governor who might refuse to carry out the monetary policies of the government of the day.
Then Mr. Rasminsky spoke of the technical arrangements, of which he sought improvement, for the exercise of monetary control by the Bank of Canada. This is by the institution of statutory secondary reserves about which I must confess I am not yet convinced in spite of all of the persuasive advocacy of the governor. To me this is adding a surplus of power to a surplus of power.

There is no doubt, Mr. Chairman, that within the statutory reserves, and particularly the statutory reserves which are embodied in the amendment to the proposed section 72 of the new Bank Act, the twelve and four formula, the effect of the 12 per cent requirement is felt on demand deposits. To me this is an extraordinarily effective weapon, and because of the changing picture of Canada's banking system as a result of the growth of a number of near banks and other financial institutions-a matter which we will be discussing when we reach the Bank Act-the Bank of Canada has less and less control over the monetary system of this country. It is trying to maintain the same level of control through the chartered banks by measures which will be and which will have to be all the more radical in their effect on the chartered banks. In other words, the basis of the exercise of this control is being narrowed as our financial system in this country evolves, and this proposal of the government to me compounds the difficulties.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
I find that the provision for statutory secondary reserves is piling super-caution upon caution and it is not at all necessary. I spoke to the minister concerning the situation in the United States where the federal reserve board has the statutory power of varying the reserve requirement up or down in order to affect the monetary policy of the country. In Canada, as we know, it is a question merely of the Bank of Canada making more money available or restricting the amount of money in circulation. This has some effect on the bond market and it also affects the interest rate.
I would have thought, in addition to the power that the Bank of Canada has to affect the monetary situation in the country through this particular procedure, there should have been an amendment to the Bank of Canada Act to allow for a variation in the primary reserve rate, particularly in connection with deposits on a fixed or term basis.

I would have thought that in addition to the power to affect the quantum of money there should have been an alternative procedure open to the Bank of Canada to affect the monetary situation in the country by allowing the bank to reduce reserves below the level indicated in the act. I hope when the minister replies he will comment upon the sufficiency of the powers at the disposal of the U.S. Federal Reserve Board, in relation to the Canadian monetary system, and whether we can add this particular tool of monetary control to our system.
This is the extent of my general remarks and I thank the committee for allowing me to make them. After all, the amendment called for by clause 1 is very limited. I hope we can get further comment from the minister, either in reply to these remarks or at the appropriate time when we are considering the clauses.

Mr. Chairman, I do not intend to take too much of the time of the committee. I do not believe there is a great deal to be said about this bill because its purpose is to clear up some anachronisms. Unlike the hon. member for Edmonton West, I do not believe clause 6 can be interpreted as a club with which the government may beat the governor of the Bank of Canada. Rather, I suspect it is a club the governor of the Bank of Canada insisted upon having placed in his hands in order to beat the Minister of Finance of the day over the head. Certainly this is the view I take of it. I must say this particular minister has never done so but, having heard a number of his predecessors dodge their responsibilities by telling the House of Commons that, after all, they could do nothing because the matter was in the hands of the Bank of Canada, I suggest that neither this minister nor his successors will be able to do so now. Any attempt to do so will meet condign punishment, I am sure, from whatever opposition there is in this chamber.
As I say, I believe the hon. member for Edmonton West has it the wrong way around. I would not be surprised if the governor of

the Bank of Canada had written that particular section himself. I regret I was not in attendance at the committee on finance and economic affairs when the Bank of Canada Act came before it. I had previously asked Mr. Rasminsky if he would be prepared to give us some information with regard to the role that the Bank of Canada plays in some of the conversations regarding reform of the international monetary system. I was hoping, as I told Mr. Rasminsky, that this might provide an opportunity for him to give at least some elementary education to myself and other members of the committee about what is going to be the next vexing question in monetary affairs. However, we can perhaps hope to get another opportunity to have the governor give us some information on that matter.
There is one thing I should like to stress now which perhaps is not truly linked to this bill. I ask the minister if he would not sound out the governor of the Bank of Canada and his staff as to the possibility of publishing some of the results of their research. I am informed the bank has collected one of the ablest stables of economists in the country who do a tremendous amount of research whose results stay in the bank or possibly go to a few selected people. If this information were made available to the public I think it would be useful in enabling the Canadian public and members of parliament to understand better the operations of our monetary system.
Beyond this, I have nothing to say about the bill. As I say, it clears up a lot of anachronisms. My seatmate, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, was rather regretful when he read that the phrase "will pay to bearer on demand" was being removed. He has always cherished the idea that one day he would take a dollar bill to the Bank of Canada and ask for a dollar for it. Now this opportunity is gone and he says that is the difficulty with postponing things. This is one of the anachronisms that has been cleared up. I think we can accept the bill as it is without further ado.

Mr. Chairman, we have
before us the proposed amendments to the

Bank of Canada Act and my question of privilege-I will hasten to say-is to the effect that French speaking hon. members in this house do not have the same opportunity to discuss these amendments as those whose mother tongue is English.
Let me explain my question of privilege. All these amendments to the Bank of Canada Act have been examined in committee. The evidence heard is contained in various numbers of committee hearing reports. You will note, Mr. Chairman, that the numbers containing the committee proceedings have only been printed in English. We have not yet received the French version. The French text is twelve numbers behind, since we have only received the French up to No. 41, whereas No. 53 of the English has been printed and distributed.
The amendments to the Bank of Canada Act had been disclosed in committee when No. 53 was published; it is still only available in English. At that time, we were discussing Bill No. C-222 and the amendments to the Chartered Banks Act. We have the English version of the minutes with respect to the clause by clause study of Bill No. C-190. However, we do not yet have these in French, since the French version of the reports on committee proceedings only go as far as January 31, 1967.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I submit that we are at a disadvantage. I know that my colleague, the hon. member for Compton-Frontenac (Mr. Latulippe), followed committee discussions very diligently. Under ordinary circumstances, it would be his turn to speak, after the Conservative party spokesman and the representative of the New Democratic Party. I am sure that he and I could express our views much more clearly if we had French transcripts of the proceedings, but we do not have them.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I feel that under the present circumstances, discussion of Bill No. C-190 should be postponed until we have received the French version of the proceedings of committee discussions.
I should like to put forward two arguments in support of my request, Mr. Chairman. My first argument is the fact that French is supposed to be an official language in this house, on a level with English. Since the proceedings are not available in the two official languages, the Minister of Finance and Receiver General (Mr. Sharp) should himself ask that consideration of the said bill be postponed until we receive the French version of the proceedings,

March 9, 1967
Bank of Canada Act
at least those concerning Bill No. C-190 which has been studied in committee.
I also wish to refer to a precedent established in this house two or three years ago, when we were considering the Canada Pension Plan or the Canada Pension Act.
It will be recalled that, at the time, a group of members pressed for postponement of examination of the Canada pension bill until such time as the proceedings on examination of the bill in committee were distributed to us in both languages.
At that time, also, we had received in English only, the reports concerning the study in committee of the Canada Pension Plan.
And, at that time, the government had graciously agreed-thereby establishing a precedent-to postpone the study of the Pension Act until such time as we would be provided with the reports in both languages. And I recall very clearly that, at that time, the government acted quickly and, in less than 24 hours, we received the reports. In less than 24 or 36 hours, if my memory serves me right, we received the reports in French, since we already had them in English, and the study of the Canada Pension Act, or the Canada pension plan, had been postponed until we received the French translation of the committee reports.
Mr. Chairman, since it has always been said that both languages, French and English, are official in this house, and since we have received the reports in one language only and it is very important for a proper discussion of the amendments to Bill No. C-190, which is a very important bill, to have the documents in French and English to be able to discuss them better, and since a denial of those documents would be an obvious discrimination against the members who speak French as their first language, and since a precedent has already been established in that respect and the present government had accepted to establish that precedent, in those circumstances, I would ask the Minister of Finance and Receiver General to agree to the postponement of the study of Bill No. C-190, as did his colleague who is today the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), until we have the reports in both languages.
I shall ask him to move the postponement of the study of Bill No. C-190 until we have the reports in both languages. I think we could get unanimous consent in that respect.

I understand that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) is the spokesman for his party as far as this bill is concerned. He will also agree no doubt, since that procedure was followed at the time of the study of the bill concerning the Canada Pension Plan, that we postpone the study of Bill No. C-190 until we have the said reports in both languages.
I shall ask the Minister of Finance and Receiver General to move himself that the study of this bill be postponed. I know that it will not be very long before we have those reports in French, and it will avoid that kind of discrimination the government does not want to have in this house.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING DIRECTION OF MONETARY POLICY, CASH RESERVES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I regret just as much as does the hon. member for Lapointe that we do not have before us at this time a complete set of the reports of the committee on finance, trade and economic affairs. The principal reason for this situation is the diligence of the committee. This committee has given a more thorough examination to the bank acts than has ever been given by any committee, I believe, in the past and this has taken a great deal of time.
The hon. member for Lapointe has himself contributed very extensively to these debates and I am sure that he would like to see his contribution before us in both languages. Unfortunately this has not been possible. Had the committee been able to complete its hearings some weeks ago we would now have these reports before us.
The position in which we now find ourselves is that we must deal fully with these bills both in this house and in the Senate, so that they may receive royal assent before April 1. If we were to delay consideration of them now in order that these reports might be available in French as well as in English, something which we would all like to see, it would be necessary for parliament to extend once again the present acts. He said; Mr. Speaker, in opening the debate on second reading of this bill it might be useful if I were to say a few more words of

explanation to enable hon. members to have a better understanding of what is proposed and how it compares with present arrangements which will expire at the end of the month.
First, on the joint use of tax fields. Parliament is being asked to increase the general abatement of the federal individual income tax from 24 to 28 percentage points and the abatement of the corporation income tax from 9 to 10 per cent of corporate profits. As I explained when moving the resolution preceding this bill, this action is proposed to enable the provincial governments to make corresponding increases in their income taxes to help meet the rising costs of higher education. Parliament is also being asked to continue the present arrangements under which the provinces receive the equivalent of 75 per cent of the yield of the federal estate tax and to extend for two more years the agreements we have with nine provinces under which the federal government collects on their behalf the income taxes they impose. Thus the change in the arrangements concerning the division of tax fields is the reduction of the federal personal income tax by four percentage points and the reduction of the federal corporation income tax by one per cent of corporate profits. If the provinces ultimately were to accept the federal offer in respect of the continuing and well-established health and welfare shared-cost programs, the general abatement of the federal personal income tax would be further increased to 5 percentage points.
Second, a fundamental reform of the equalization arrangements is being proposed. Under existing arrangements the per capita yields of the personal and corporation income taxes and the estate tax at standard rates of taxation are equalized to the level of the top two provinces and then a deduction is made in the case of provinces whose natural resources revenues are above average. In addition, special grants, the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants, are paid to the four Atlantic provinces. These grants were originally paid in amounts equal to an approximation of the amount required to equalize the yield, at national average rates, from all provincial-municipal revenue sources other than those already included in the general equalization formula, up to 85 per cent of the national average.
* (5:10 p.m.)
The equalization formula proposed in this bill differs from the existing arrangements
March 9, 1967	COMMONS
in three important respects. First, it is based on a comprehensive index of the relative fiscal capacities of the provinces and takes all provincial revenues into account. Second, it is sensitive to the revenue requirements of the provinces taken together and to changes in the relative tax capacity of the individual provinces. Third it takes into account objective factors only; transitional problems are dealt with in special transitional arrangements.
If hon. members will refer to the two tables which were placed in Hansard of March 2, pages 13684 to 13687, it will be observed that for purposes of calculating equalization payments provincial revenues have been grouped into 16 classes. As indicated in Table 1, pages 13684 and 13685, the tax or revenue base for each class of revenue is identified and determined for each province and for all the provinces together. Having determined the revenue base for each revenue source, the amount of revenue derived from each source by all provinces is determined. The total of provincial revenues for each revenue source is then applied to the total appropriate revenue base to determine the national average provincial revenue rate for each source.
In brief, the average provincial "tax rate" for corporation income tax, the average provincial tax per gallon for gasoline, the average provincial sales tax rate, etc., is determined, and this average provincial tax rate is applied to the appropriate revenue base in each province to calculate the revenue each province would derive from its own revenue base at this provincial average tax rate. The total potential revenue available to each province from all provincial sources, at average provincial tax rates, is then converted into per capita terms for comparative purposes.
If the total potential per capita revenue for a province is below the per capita total for all provinces, that province will be entitled to an equalization payment equal to the difference. The total payment, as indicated in line 8(b) of Table II, pages 13686 and 13687 of Hansard, will be the product of the per capita deficiency multiplied by the population of the province.
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that I am describing this like the announcer on the radio in the morning who is trying to convince us that the simplified tax forms are indeed very simple. However, I think it will be better understood on reading than on listening.
Equalization Payments to Provinces
On applying this formula to provincial data it was found that six provinces would be entitled to equalization and four provinces, Ontario, British Columbia, Alberta, and Saskatchewan, would not. To enable the province of Saskatchewan, which will receive equalization grants amounting to about $33 million in 1966-67, to make an orderly transition to its new status, provision is made to phase out Saskatchewan's current equalization entitlement over the five-year life of the new arrangements.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister indicated in the course of his remarks that the found the formula he was trying to explain much like the new simplified tax form that we have to fill out. I think he is minimizing the difficulties facing hon. members generally in respect of really analysing the bill to see who is to gain and to assess the value of the government's proposal. We recall that last autumn at the dominion-provincial conference there was a tremendous uproar from the representatives of the provinces because they felt that the proposal then put forward by the federal government was not even understood by the representatives of the federal government. Since that time the Minister of Finance (Mr. 
DEBATES	March 9. 1967
Sharp) and his staff have had an opportunity to really study all the implications, as have the provinces.
At the outset I must say I find it rather singular that last autumn the provinces cried to high heaven that they were being maltreated. There was a great performance all around. As a matter of fact, there were real histrionics. Since then, however, there has been a deadly silence. Although the bill has been published since March 3 we have not heard much, if anything at all, from the provinces concerning its effect. True enough, there is one, I suppose, who might be deemed to have benefited from the objectives he raised in view of the provision in clause 9 of the bill with regard to Saskatchewan transitional payments. I am wondering whether we should call it "Thatcher's Soothing Syrup". It does provide for some easing of the change with regard to Saskatchewan. I do not know whether this is an attempt to try to blight the cause of the premier of that province who seems to delight in raking the backs of his colleagues in Ottawa from time to time. I am not going to go into, shall we say, the period of transition in his political philosophies from when he sat with hon. members on the left to the position he now occupies where he seems to be in the Liberal right.
Some years ago at the time we went through a mammoth exercise when the minister's predecessor was in office we had presented to us with a great fanfare of trumpets, as though it was really the epitome of co-operative federalism, a bill called the Established Programs (Interim Arrangements) Act. I remember that the hon. member for Nanai-mo-Cowichan-The Islands (Mr. Cameron) and I characterized that bill as the smallest mouse the mountain had ever produced in its most difficult labours, because it did nothing. Lo and behold, it does nothing again today. All it does is confer on one province an extension of the famous opting out formula in part. Mind you, when we consider the bill clause by clause in detail I think the minister had better explain just what it all means and whether it is limited or applies to all joint programs. In essence, however, it does indicate that it applies to any program commencing after September 30, 1967. We will get around to that.
As I said, I still think that earlier legislation was the biggest fraud perpetrated on the Canadian public as being a new formula for granting the provinces fiscal rights. Under that act they had no more rights than they
March 9, 19S7
ever had in so far as these particular programs were concerned. They were still tied to the agreements and are now still tied to the joint program agreements. There are no relaxations at all. The only thing is that the one province, the province of Quebec, which has availed itself of the provisions may feel it is getting squatters' rights with regard to certain tax revenues. That, of course, will be something for the future to decide. I am trusting that there will be some amicable form of arrangement, because if there is not there will be a cataclysmic collision between the two governmental authorities and we will be in for a difficult time. If such is to be our fate, we may just be postponing the evil day. I trust that this will not be the case and that we will be able to work it out.
I agree that there is to be some sort of reallocation of the sources of funds between the federal government and the provinces. Just what the formula is is hard to define. It is worthy of note that the provinces and their municipalities now spend far more money than the federal government. Obviously this bill is the incarnation into a statute of a principle that was enunciated back in 1961 when the prior dominion-provincial agreement was negotiated, that is, if the provinces want to spend money, then let them tax for it. I think this is a sound and fundamental principle and I agree with it. Those provinces which wish to carry on at a higher level than some of their counterparts in the remainder of Canada can legislate and face up to the realities of imposing the taxes for the money they wish to spend. They have this right. The then minister of finance and the government were severely criticized for imposing this upon the provinces but, as I say, like Paul on the way to Tarsus the present administration became converted to this fact and now really is putting it into force with a vengeance.
One question on which the minister did not touch has to do with clause 5. This will be my only reference to that clause. It deals with the basic estate tax, its definition and what happens to succession duties. I should like to hear what the minister has to say about the proposal contained in the statute introduced for first reading in the legislature of the province of Alberta the other day in which power is given to the province to repay-this is a novel way to do it-to the administrators, trustees, or successors of an estate up to 75 per cent of the estate tax that has been paid. Presumably this is an initial step to create Alberta as an estate tax haven.
Equalization Payments to Provinces
How will this affect this particular agreement? How will it affect the relationship with the other provinces? As a matter of fact, I think the province of British Columbia has similar legislation before its legislature. Perhaps it is not exactly the same in detail but it has the same aim. We will find, of course, that a number of other provinces will follow this example. How is this going to affect these agreements? After all, the agreement is for five years. Much can happen in that time in relation to succession duties, and the balance of payments to provinces may be completely upset. What then will be the result?
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
In concluding my remarks on second reading I should like to protest once more against what I think is a fundamental error in the determination of revenue source. I made this protest at the time of the passing of the Established Programs (Interim Arrangements) Act. I have specific reference to federal-provincial fiscal arrangements in relation to the determination of what moneys obtained by the provinces from the sale of crown leases and reserves on oil and natural gas lands shall be deemed to be revenue. This is fundamentally wrong because the sale of crown leases and reserves is in effect the alienation of capital assets.
It is true that revenue can come from royalties but the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan have objected strenuously to the oil and gas revenue feature being incorporated in the formula in earlier years. I remember that the hon. member for Burna-by-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) also objected very strongly. The principles behind our arguments at that time apply equally today. I cannot for the life of me see why something which is in essence the sale of an asset should be considered revenue. In that event one might say that in a certain regard the province of Alberta would be acting like the prodigal son. I think a fundamental mistake has been made in this regard because of the budgeting philosophy of the province of Alberta which has always considered the proceeds from the sale of leases and reserves on oil and natural gas lands in the same way Saskatchewan considers the sale of leases on phosphates. If these were bonus considerations, that would be one thing, but these are sales of capital assets and it is fundamentally wrong to incorporate them in any revenue picture. This would be a method of financing

13792	COMMONS
Equalization Payments to Provinces a spendthrift or a person going into bankruptcy. One must believe that one could live off the proceeds of the disposal of capital assets.
Certainly this whole question involves millions and millions of dollars for the province of Alberta and has involved a great deal each year for the past ten years. This has altered the revenues of that province. I cannot understand why the proceeds from the sale of crown leases and reserves on oil and natural gas lands should be included as a revenue source.
I trust that other members of the house will express their views on this point and I hope the minister will give us a detailed explanation of why this is being done. It is my suggestion to the minister that this is working an injustice on the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and to some extent British Columbia. I do agree that royalties should be considered as revenue because they are obtained over a period of years but I cannot understand the inclusion of bonus considerations on auction sales of crown leases and reserves. I hope we will be given some explanation.
In respect of this bill we are again faced with the five minute to midnight situation. We are being asked to pass this bill because the present agreement expires on March 31. A conference was held in this regard in September and I wonder why the bill was not introduced long before now in order that we could carry out a thorough study of it. The adoption of this bill will determine for several years the division of revenues between the federal government and the provinces, and I think it is almost contemptuous of parliament to ask us to pass it at this late stage. Had it not been for the accidental rising and reporting of progress of the committee in respect of Bill C-190 we would not now be dealing with this bill. Probably we would not have dealt with it until much later this month after we had considered the Bank Act.
I cannot let this opportunity pass without vehemently protesting against the comtempti-ble attitude the government has shown toward parliament. This action embellishes the image of this minister vis-a-vis that of one of his colleagues who wants one uniform and one rank structure. In my opinion this measure is far more important than Bill C-243. With those remarks, Mr. Speaker, I wish now to let others indicate how dissatisfied we are with the timing of this measure and some of its features.

Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that this bill has been brought on suddenly before we have had an opportunity to study it in detail. The resolution preceding the bill was only passed the other day and there are a great many details we need before making a complete assessment of the bill. It was my hope that we would be given a more detailed statement by the ministers concerned than we have been given today. Perhaps after we look at the two tables the minister put on the record we may get some further information.
Having regard to the bill before us and the statement of the minister let me raise several objections. The first is that the new equalization formula will equalize grants to provinces to the level of the national average whereas in the past they were equalized to the average of the two top provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES
speechtext: In respect of two sources of tax.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yes, in respect of two
sources of taxes. But many of us have argued for a long time that they ought to be equalized to the top province. However, we have settled for an average of the two top provinces. The minister now intends to base the equalization payment on the national average. This will destroy much of the value we estimated would result from the equalization formula.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
Let me remind the house that if one reads the Rowell-Sirois report one finds that its whole concept, was that the federal government should collect the three main taxes, income tax, corporation tax and succession duties, and that this pool of tax revenue ought to be divided, after the federal government had taken out its share, among the provinces on the basis of need. This was the fundamental concept. The concept of that report was that payments should be made to the provinces in order to bring them up to a level of services for education, health and welfare that would make for uniformity across Canada. The concept of the Rowell-Sirois report was that a Canadian, irrespective of the geographic area in which he or she might live, was entitled to a certain standard of health, welfare and educational services commensurate with the level of services enjoyed by Canadians in other parts of the country.
Successive governments, of course, have never lived up to this principle of need. What we have done instead is to work out an
March 9, 1967	COMMONS
equalization formula designed to mitigate the worst discrepancies that obtain between the various regions of Canada. I submit that the equalization formula now before the house is certainly not going to eliminate the existing regional disparities. The minister says, of course, that the total amount for equalization grants is larger. That is true; it is higher in total by some $140 million. But I would point out that in connection with the $494 million in equalization payments one province will receive almost half, namely, $235,282,000. I am not complaining about that but it will do little to remove the disparity that exists in some of the other provinces. When one sees that the province of Newfoundland will receive $59.8 million, Prince Edward Island $14 million, Nova Scotia $69 million, New Brunswick $60 million and Manitoba $29 million, one realizes that this formula will do little to enable the people in the have-not provinces to enjoy the same level of services that is enjoyed by people in other parts of the country.
I understand it is the intention to eliminate the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants. If those grant are eliminated, of course, the special consideration which was being given to the Atlantic provinces will be removed. I am fearful that the minister is thinking purely in financial and budgetary terms and has lost sight of the original principle of equalization which was to eliminate as far as possible the discrepancies which obtain between the revenue of some parts of Canada and others and their ability to provide their people with adequate services.
I noticed that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) said that the provinces should impose the taxes for the money which they want to spend. This, I take it, is the principle upon which the minister is proceeding. That seems logical in theory. The fact is that there are provinces in Canada which do not have the tax base from which revenue can be derived. There are provinces in Canada that, no matter what taxes they impose, cannot possibly of their own accord give to their people a level of services that would in any way be related to the services provided in the wealthier provinces. The whole purpose of equalization was to recognize this fact, to recognize that much of the money collected by the federal government is collected from corporations which are located in certain provinces but make their money in other parts of Canada, and that the money,
Equalization Payments to Provinces although it is collected in the wealthier provinces, is not all earned in those wealthier provinces but is earned as a result of the effort of all the people of Canada and by doing business in every part of Canada.
I am fearful that the reducing of the equalization formula to the national average is moving in the wrong direction. For a while it was based on the national average. The provinces felt it was a significant gain to be able to get equalization to the two top provinces, and we hoped that eventually we would get equalization to the top province and thus we would bring the other provinces up to the level of the highest income province in Canada. Now we are taking a retrograde step and going back to the national average.
My second objection to this legislation is that it completely ignores municipal revenue. I think that the government in its equalization formula would have been wiser to have stayed with even the three original sources of revenue that were in the agreement preceding the one now in existence. But if the government is going to take into account all forms of provincial revenue it ought to go one step further and include municipal revenue, because there is a wide variation among the provinces in the division of responsibilities between the respective provinces and their municipalities. Some provinces spend more money to help their municipalities and their school boards, and provide services which in other provinces have to be supplied to a greater extent by the municipalities. I feel that the government has ignored this factor completely, which will further accentuate the discrepancies that are bound to occur between provinces.
My third objection to this legislation is that it is concentrated solely on the revenue side of the equation and takes no account of the variations in the cost of providing services in different parts of Canada. The cost of providing services in some parts of Canada is considerably higher than in other parts of this country. I think the minister, in basing an equalization formula solely on the total average tax yields across Canada, has overlooked this important point.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
My fourth objection has to do with the desirability of including all forms of provincial revenue in computing equalization grants. I remind the house that originally equalization was based on the revenues which a province received from three fields of taxation, namely, income tax, corporation tax and succession duties. In arguing the case when
13794	COMMONS DEBATES	March 9, 1967
Equalization Payments to Provinces
the present formula was introduced I for one opposed including revenue from resource development, and I am still opposed to it. I am opposed to including it for two reasons. First, as has already been pointed out, revenue from resource development is a declining asset; it is not a recurring revenue. It is revenue from oil, from minerals of various kinds and from timber, much of which is not renewed. Timber if properly managed can be renewable, but oil, gas and minerals are not renewable assets and as they are used up the revenue will decline. To use this as one of the factors in determining equalization payments seems to me to be most unfair.
The other reason why I do not think revenue from resource development should be included is that the minister is taking into consideration the gross revenue. If a province succeeds in getting revenue from oil, potash, sodium sulphate, copper, lead, zinc, coal or any of the minerals that are mined in a province, that province must spend very large sums of money to bring about that development. It must spend money on geophysical surveys, on exploratory work and on building roads into these areas. Therefore if the minister must include the revenues from resource development in computing the equalization formula, surely it should at least be a net figure and not a gross figure. The result of including not only resource development revenue but all revenue for the province and taking the national average means that we are getting what I think will be a very unfair distribution of revenue to the provinces and I think it will create a great many anomalies and discrepancies.
The minister has mentioned the province of Saskatchewan. He said he is very pleased that Saskatchewan is a "have" province. If he took the trouble to look at the figures he would find that Saskatchewan has been a "have" province for a great many years. Saskatchewan's per capita income has been above the national average for a long time. He would also find that the resource revenue which is coming in now is coming in from potash mines and oil wells most of which were established prior to 1964. So the situation which faces Saskatchewan today is not much different from what it was when the present agreement was signed. The only difference is that, first of all, resource development is now being included, whereas in previous agreements prior to the one now in effect resource development was not included, and I do not think it should be. Second,

while Saskatchewan's resource revenue is increasing as potash mines come into production, no account is taken of the fact that the province of Saskatchewan has had to spend very large sums of money in order to get this revenue.
The minister is going to give to Saskatchewan and also to Prince Edward Island, if I remember correctly, a sort of guaranteed equalization grant which will help them to phase out this situation. However, I do not think that is the answer. The fact that Saskatchewan is going to get some $8 million less out of this formula than it got out of previous formulae is not so much because Saskatchewan is a great deal better off financially but because it is dealing with a Minister of Finance who has changed the rules of the game. The formula he is now imposing upon the provinces is one which is designed to work against those provinces which have spent large sums of money in order to get resource development, and no account is being taken of the sums of money which they have spent for that purpose.
I close by saying that I hope that before we get into committee of the whole the Minister of Finance will give us some of the figures which I understand have been compiled by the tax structure committee. I referred to this matter when the resolution was before the house the other day. I want to ask the minister if the tax structure committee made an estimate which showed that, on the basis of an annual increase in the gross national product of some 7 per cent, by 1972 the federal government will have a surplus of $727 million and the municipalities and the provinces will have a deficit of some $2,100 million.
I also want to know whether on the basis of a 6 per cent annual growth in the gross national product the federal government will still have a surplus by 1972 and the provinces and municipalities will have an estimated deficit of $2,100 millions. It is important that we have this information because I think that we in the house have to be concerned about what this agreement will do for the provinces and municipalities. The provinces and municipalities have to provide certain services. They are the only bodies which have the constitutional authority to provide such services as education, health and welfare and municipal services such as water, sewers, etc. If they are not able to provide those services, then irrespective of whether or not the federal government has a surplus the people of Canada will have a low standard of
March 9, 1967

life and young people of Canada will be deprived of educational opportunities and opportunities for good health, adequate hospital facilities and the other things which are required. I think that the minister should give us that information.
This house must be concerned about what this very rigid agreement is going to do to the provinces and the municipalities and to what extent it will limit their capacity to provide the services which they are required to provide. If over the course of the next five years the municipalities and provincial governments have to curtail services, then it means that the people of Canada are going to have a lower standard of living. I say to the minister that with the Carter report having just come out and with the whole question of taxation being considered he might be well advised to look into the possibility of a shorter term for these agreements. I must confess that I am seriously worried about a five-year agreement formulated on the basis of a tax structure that the Carter report has shown to be markedly inequitable. If this agreement is imposed on the provinces for the next five years, the fiscal changes which will be necessary in this country will not benefit them to the extent that they ought.
[DOT] (6:00 p.m.)
I see you are going to call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker, and I have completed my remarks. I simply want to ask the minister whether, when we come to the committee stage, he will give us some of the information that has been collected by the tax structure committee.
