subtopic: SUBJECT MATTER OF QUESTIONS TO BE DEBATED
speechtext:
That an order of the house do issue for a copy of all correspondence, telegrams or other documents, dated since January 1,	1961, exchanged
between the Secretary of State or any agency or department of the government of Canada relating to payments made to John T. Saywell and/or John C. Ricker by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and a list setting out in detail each such payment to each such person.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in moving this motion for the production of papers which has just been read by Your Honour I would point out that I would not have had the temerity to move a motion asking for information from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation having had many years' experience of requesting information, which requests have been met with the bland answer: "We don't give out information. Such information is not in the public interest. Such information is not divulged to parliament". They continue to ask us for money but they do not give us any information.
About two months ago Mr. Alphonse Oui-met, president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, made a statement in connection with what became known as the von Thad-den incident, during the course of which he made these remarks:
This action does not mean that the corporation will abrogate its responsibility in terms of the principle of the right of the Canadian public to information.
There, Mr. Speaker, is a flat statement if there ever was one. Mr. Ouimet said:
This action does not mean that the corporation will abrogate its responsibility in terms of the principle of the right of the Canadian public to information.
For the past 30 years or even longer the C.B.C. has been telling all questioners: "We cannot give that kind of information. It is not in the public interest. Such information is not divulged." But here is Mr. Ouimet, with big, mouth-filling words, coming down flat footed-ly on the side of truth and making the statement:
This action does not mean that the corporation will abrogate its responsibility in terms of the principle of the right of the Canadian public to information.
The information that I want, Mr. Speaker, is how much money has been paid by the C.B.C. to Professor John T. Saywell and/or

March 9, 1967
Motions for Papers
John C. Ricker, another teacher in Toronto, by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation year by year for the last five years.
I was strengthened in my expectation that there had been a tremendous volte-face by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as outlined by Mr. Ouimet in his press release of January 16, 1967, because Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), who answers in parliament for the C.B.C. and, as I have pointed out before, in fact does not make any answer but just represents the C.B.C. in the house, in commenting on the von Thadden incident had this to say. You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that there was an outcry against the C.B.C. for spending the Canadian public's money bringing this man to this country, and as reported at page 11819 of Hansard the Secretary of State stated:
But there is the principle of respecting the right of the Canadian people to know what is current in the world-
If there is the principle of respecting the right of the Canadian people to know what is current in the world, I should like to know how much money has been paid to Professor John T. Saywell and John C. Ricker; and I think that I am looking for information to which the public is entitled because it is taxpayers' money that is being put into the pockets of these two gentlemen.
Picking this incident concerning Mr. Say-well and Mr. Ricker as the peg on which to hang my motion, Mr. Speaker, in view of these two flatfooted statements by Mr. Ouimet and the Secretary of State in which I presume we are supposed to place some reliance, even though it may be falsely placed, my interest in ascertaining how much money has been paid to Messrs. Saywell and Ricker has been triggered by the fact that in a book jointly authored by the two of them entitled "Nation and Province" which has been circulated among the schools of Ontario by the Ontario department of education there were some very sharp attacks on the printed word.
I have been engaged in the publishing world for 40 years and have a very high respect for Canadian publishers. Messrs. Saywell and Ricker collected money from the C.B.C. by expressing opinions from time to time, many of which have no doubt come to the attention of hon. members. However, in their book "Nation and Province", under the heading of "Parliament and the Press" they go out of their way to point out that there are some dangerous tendencies in the world of the printed press, one being a dangerous

tendency toward centralization. This book was published about eight years ago, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps one reason the federal government is leaning toward decentralization more than ever before is that Messrs. Saywell and Ricker have referred to the dangerous tendency toward centralization.
Let me repeat what I said in this house on February 10. Who says that centralization is dangerous, Mr. Speaker? In the publishing world in Canada more and more publications are joining what are known as the great chains. Those of us who have had experience in the publishing world in Canada cannot see that there is a dangerous tendency in that regard. Many of these publications would not be in existence today had they not sold out to a chain operator, as a result of which they get the economies of mass buying and come under the brilliant management of people who are, without question, first class operators. As a result a publication that singly might have foundered is now able to continue profitably under chain operation.
Messrs. Saywell and Ricker make reference in their book not only to the dangerous tendency toward centralization but also talk about whether people can believe the news which is published in our papers. The interesting thing is that they praise the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. They point out that newspapers may well be reluctant to print news or opinions which could have an adverse effect on advertising interests.
I should like to ask Professor Saywell and Mr. Ricker for their comments with regard to some newspapers I could name that are owned by very large corporation which are among the biggest advertisers in the whole Dominion of Canada. I think in particular of one paper owned and controlled by the largest advertiser in Canada, about which Professor Saywell and Mr. Ricker might tell us you cannot believe a word this publication prints because its ownership rests in the hands of an advertiser. But, Mr. Speaker, this does not automatically make you a liar, or open to criticism, or convict you of being unable to tell the truth. I submit that the statement of Messrs. Saywell and Ricker is absolutely uncalled for.
[DOT] (6:10 p.m.)
But having accepted money from the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation they go on to make their case on a comparison with private newspapers and private radio stations
March 9. 1967

and on page 60 of their book, "Nation and Province", I find the following:
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, owned by the government and the people of Canada, does an admirable job in keeping the public informed on events in parliament; being the servant of public rather than private interests, its news is impartial.
This is quite an interesting statement for these gentlemen to be making. The money they have received from the C.B.C. in the past has of course, never influenced their judgment. They, of course, would be the last people in the world to extend any modicum of thanks to someone who had benefited them in a pecuniary way, such as the C.B.C.
Then we have the attack made by Knowlton Nash of the C.B.C. on August 11 in a C.B.C. broadcast against these nefarious newspaper people. I have in my hand an exact transcript of the comments made by Mr. Knowlton Nash from Washington as supplied to me by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation itself. It does seem to me that the C.B.C. spends much of its time trying to cast reflections on United States' action in Viet Nam. If there is the slightest tittle of information they can pick up that might reflect on United States' action in Viet Nam, the C.B.C. gives it national coverage. In this statement which I hold in my hand, and which is just the way the C.B.C. gave it to me, I find the following:
Today, one hundred United States servicemen answered a call for blood donors sent out by the hospital in Cam Tho. And teams of American and South Vietnamese doctors and nurses have been sent there to care for the injured civilians.
In Washington, C.B.C. correspondent Knowlton Nash reports that authorities there are becoming concerned at the "bad press" the United States is receiving in some countries over her actions in Viet Nam.
That was the introduction, and now we have Knowlton Nash, the voice of authority, the voice of righteousness, the voice of correct opinions, saying:
The United States has been getting increasingly alarmed lately at the somewhat less than enthusiastic support given to U.S. actions in Viet Nam by reporters in Canada, France, the United Kingdom and other countries.
The United States must be greatly upset over the fact that reporters in Canada, France and the United Kingdom do not support them.
To try to rectify this so-called "bad press" the U.S. information service has come up with a rather traditional press agent approach. It's flying free to Saigon specially selected editors and commentators from other countries ... including three Canadian newsmen.
Motions for Papers
The U.S. agency says that it does not want to identify the newsmen because it says this might lessen their credibility.
This statement, of course, is being made on the C.B.C. national network by a C.B.C. employee in an effort to discredit the three newsmen who had accepted an invitation to be flown to Viet Nam to see what is going on with their own eyes so they can give an accurate report to the Canadian public. These three newsmen were later identified. I identified them in my remarks on February 10. Toward the end of his statement Mr. Knowlton Nash says:
The Post says some Canadian newspapers have turned down the free trip preferring, as the C.B.C. has done, to pay their own way for their correspondents.
He refers to the C.B.C., that guardian of the truth in Canada. What about Miss Beryl Fox of the C.B.C., who went to Viet Nam to report on the situation there? The C.B.C. may have paid her way to South Viet Nam, but everybody in this chamber knows that she could not have seen anything in Viet Nam if the United States government had not made transportation available to her throughout the length and breadth of that country. She took advantage of the hospitality of the United States government and toured South Viet Nam. She comes back here and over the C.B.C. comments unfavourably on the attitudes and actions of the United States government in South Viet Nam.
If Mr. Knowlton Nash feels that the gentlemen who accepted the hospitality of the United States government and made visits to Viet Nam cannot be believed because they have accepted this hospitality, then why does he not condemn the Canadian cabinet which invites people to come here to look this country over and form an opinion about what is going on in Canada? I have in my hand a photostat record of people coming to Canada at government expense. By the way, Mr. J. Hourie, editor of the Jerusalem Post, is in the city of Ottawa at the present time at the expense of the Canadian government. If there is something the matter with people accepting expense paid trips across the Pacific Ocean to South Viet Nam, then is there not something the matter with the Canadian government bringing people into this country? Are we trying to influence their judgment? Does this mean that when they go back to their countries the people cannot believe them because they have been influenced by the hospitality of the Canadian government?

March 9, 1967
Motions for Papers
I have a clipping from the Ottawa Citizen dated February 25 which reads:
Erik Blumenfeld, chairman of the West German Bundestag's (Parliament's) Vietnam subcommittee, will speak to the Council of Foreign Relations in New York Tuesday, it was announced Friday.
He then will visit Montreal and Ottawa at the invitation of the Canadian Institute of Public Affairs.
Is the Canadian Institute of Public Affairs trying to influence this man's judgment? If they are not, why are they bringing him over here? If all these newsmen who visit South Viet Nam at the invitation of the United States government are to have their credibility called into question, then how does it come about that when the Canadian government fly C.B.C. equipment, cameramen and commentators all over this country and in many cases across oceans to distant parts of the world, the C.B.C. does not state, do not believe us; we have been influenced by the munificence of the Canadian government toward the C.B.C? If the C.B.C. believes what Knowlton Nash, a paid employee of that organization, is saying, then why does not the C.B.C. pay its own expenses in sending cameramen and commentators wherever the C.B.C. may desire instead of participating in the generosity of the Canadian government? This is certainly a case of the pot calling the kettle black. It is a two-faced attitude, if I ever saw one, to criticize men who have accepted the munificence of the United States government and then turn around and accept the generosity of the Canadian government.
I also have in my hand a clipping from the Ottawa Citizen dated February 4. Under a three column heading, "VIP Arrangements Under Way", there is mention of the people who are going to visit Canada during centennial year. The article is by Shirley Foley, assistant women's editor. In the article I find such phrases as, "The government's invitations have also included... "the provincial and federal governments will collaborate on these outside Ottawa visits in matters of security, hospitality, etc.". Then there is this phrase: ".. .while the Canadian government will see to their getting about within the country."
There is another article concerning the President of Zambia which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of November 18, 1966. The article states that the President of Zambia arrived in Ottawa after a flight from New York in a transport department Viscount. Later in the article I find this statement:
On Saturday, he and Mr. Martin will leave by transport department aircraft for the university convocation at Windsor.

Then we have a story in the Montreal Star of November 17, 1966, which states that a Swedish prince is in that city. The article states that the prince flew in aboard a Canadian government Viscount from Ottawa and was taken immediately to the Expo administration building on the site of the 1967 world's fair. If it is irregular and incorrect for newsmen to accept invitations from governments to visit parts of the world where the action is, then why does the Canadian government participate in such nefarious practices by asking people to come over here at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer? Does the Canadian government expect these people to accept our hospitality and then go back and knife the host country in return? This practice has been going on for hundreds of years. People who have been anxious to create a good impression have been willing to pay money to entertain those who might be commenting on the situation.
A less interesting angle of this situation is the search for the truth which the C.B.C. recently undertook when it went to great lengths to interview an 11-year-old girl. She had written a piece of poetry which appeared in a United States magazine. The poem attacked the United States action in Viet Nam. This is a religious publication which printed it. It is a small publication and this was a small contest. I said a little while ago that if the C.B.C. could find some way of attacking the actions of the United States government in South Viet Nam it would go to any lengths to do so. This is a perfect example of that. They send interviewers down to interview a little girl and reproduce this poem. However, the ideas of an 11-year-old girl on the United States government's interference in Viet Nam are not of much importance to the people of Canada. But that does not bother the C.B.C. It is the Canadian taxpayers' money they are squandering, and they are going to give the opinion of an 11-year-old girl on this affair. Why in Heaven's name cannot the C.B.C. spend its money to get the opinions of people who are knowledgeable on the subject instead of interviewing 11-year-old children?
[DOT] (6:20 p.m.)
We have three members of this House of Commons who are at this moment touring Taiwan, South Viet Nam, Indonesia and the Malay States at the expense of the governments of those countries. When they return, are we to say to them that their words cannot be believed or taken at face value because they have been influenced by the generosity
March 9, 1987

of their hosts-brainwashed by the host countries? This is what has been said of three newsmen who were attacked and held up to public ridicule by Mr. Knowlton Nash in that broadcast on August 11. 1 sincerely hope the C.B.C. will produce the information for which I asked so that you and I will be able to judge just how impartial are the opinions of the news commentators of the corporation.
I have a C.B.C. list of more than 80 newspapermen who have been paid to broadcast on C.B.C. programs such as "Pre-view", "Viewpoint" and the six o'clock news. Do you think the C.B.C. uses newsmen because the corporation has a high regard for them? Far from it. Mr. Stanley Burke, the gorgeous anchorman on the C.B.C. national television news, speaking in Toronto on March 2 at a reorganization meeting of the Sigma Delta Chi fraternity, said in the course of comments to a group of newsmen that the primary concern of the new operation was to develop an organization which would enable the C.B.C. to go after its own news rather than rehash news provided through the print media. Burke told us what he thinks of the news provided by the news media. So why do they have these newsmen appearing all the time on C.B.C. radio and television stations if they have such an opinion of the work they are doing? The answer is that they do so in order that these men will be favourably disposed toward the C.B.C. and that, as they write for the papers which employ them, they will make laudatory references to the corporation commending it for its noble work and on the vast undertaking which it is operating.
If anybody was ever paid money to get a favourable opinion it is certainly the newspapermen whose names the C.B.C. has on lists which are interminably long. But why does the C.B.C. turn around and attack Canadian newspapermen of the utmost reputation? Of the three, I have known two of them for many years and I have no hesitation about believing anything they write. When the Secretary of State makes the statement that there is a principle here which involves respect for the right of the Canadian people to know what is going on currently in the world, and when Mr. Alphonse Ouimet in connection with the von Thadden incident passes the remark that the principle of the public's right to information was involved-this was why they were going to bring the German here before they changed their minds-let me say that I too have a right to some information. There is something I want to know and it is: How much has been paid to Messrs. Saywell
Motions for Papers
and Ricker who have made these commendatory statements about the C.B.C.'s service while giving the back of their hand to the established print media which have been in business in this country for over 150 years?
Of course, there is no connection between the money they received and the laudatory things they said about the C.B.C. But I believe that as a matter of record we should know how much was paid to them and then we shall know just how impartial is the judgment of these men. Hon. members may be interested to know that the Ontario Department of Education has withdrawn the book from the schools of Ontario because of the bias shown by one medium of communication against the print media.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am of the opinion that many of the requests to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for information should be given favourable consideration. I believe that much of the misunderstanding which occurs could

March 9, 1967
Motions for Papers
be eliminated if we knew just how the corporation operates. Like many other people I have been shocked about some of the things which the C.B.C has done and I regret that it has been so difficult to get information from the corporation.
I am of the opinion that the broadcasting committee should have recommended the disposal by any means possible-retirement, promotion, or what have you-of the old strata in the C.B.C. who we found on investigation serve no function at all. They were a little like the Senators in the other place. After a politician has outworn his usefulness it is nice to have a place in which to put him. The C.B.C. has a large selection of vice presidents who might be placed in that category. Inefficiency at this level is marked, and this may be connected with the reluctance to give information which might shed light on some of the things which happen in the C.B.C.
The hon. member who has moved this motion for the production of correspondence has told us he is not particularly interested in learning the amounts of money paid to these two gentlemen. Frankly, I do not know either one of them. I think the hon. member has probably moved this motion in order to call attention to the unwillingness of top management of the C.B.C to co-operate by complying with very simple requests which do not seem to be unreasonable or even, in some cases, to contain much merit.
The C.B.C in refusing to table this type of document puts on the type of halo that it does not deserve. It is necessary for members of parliament who are particularly interested in the C.B.C to speak out about some of the abuses which the corporation perpetrates or there will be a lot of people who will say, "To hell with the C.B.C."
I am sure those who watched the coverage of the funeral ceremonies yesterday were proud of the job the corporation did on that occasion.

1 think it could not have been done nearly as well by any other agency. Part of the reason they were able to make such a good showing is, no doubt, the range and variety of equipment available as a result of the money placed by parliament at the corporation's disposal.

We have provided the C.B.C. with facilities. That being the case, how is it that with respect to northern Ontario, where sports are
fMr. Peters.]
very important, the C.B.C. is quite willing, openly and without bias or charge to provide the other networks with full coverage of a national event such as that which took place yesterday, but when C.T.V. buys the coverage rights for sports it will not allow that coverage to be carried by the C.B.C. to areas the C.T.V. cannot cover, on either a gratuity or exchange basis? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad you were able to ascertain that from the remarks made by the hon. member. I certainly was not, and I am not in a position to tell you whether these two newspapermen were not covering sports. However, I agree the debate may have extended beyond the terms of the motion and therefore I will return to it.
The motion refers specifically to two members of the press who did some work for the C.B.C. As I say, I am not prepared to state whether or not this was in the field of sports. Obviously Foster Hewitt was not involved, but I am not sure what these men did. However, I do not think the point I was trying to make is unrelated. My point was that no matter what correspondence is sought it is always considered to be privileged.
I only wish you, Mr. Speaker, had the opportunity of listening to the questioning of C.B.C. officials every time we raised matters concerning salaries and stipends paid to people working for that organization. In no case was the information given graciously or gratuitously; it was always obtained by circumvention.
March 9. 1967

When discussing this motion we must consider something else which has happened in the C.B.C. and which is not to our advantage or in the national interest. I refer to the hiring of newspaper people to do some of the jobs previously done by well known news commentators. We now have on television a new news format, introduced by people like Mr. Saywell and Mr. Ricker, dramatizing the news, leading to particular segments of news being picked out and linked together. Competition being what it is, and the C.T.V. having developed this type of format, the C.B.C. had to follow suit. We no longer see Mr. Cameron broadcasting the news in a matter of fact, factual manner. We see the dramatization of news, and this format eliminates anything that is not dramatic, and leads to the introduction of outside press people.
Because of this it is important that we know how much these people are paid because I think, due to the dramatization of the news, we are being misled in many cases. If public funds are being spent to pay these people, and if thousands of dollars are spent for short excerpts involving outside camera crews in order to dramatize certain aspects of the news, then I think it would be in the interests of the C.B.C. to make such information available and to table the correspondence that is sought in the motion before the house. But if it does table that correspondence it will lead to demands for more correspondence of this sort; everyone will want to know what everyone else, hired on an ad hoc basis, is paid.
This may lead members of parliament to say, when watching news on television, "If he got $20, that is too much." On the other hand if somebody else got $40 they may say it was probably a reasonable amount. We may say that Mr. Lynch is worth $100 an appearance on C.B.C. news and Mr. Saywell worth only $40, at which rate he may be overpaid or underpaid, depending on our own opinions. If the C.B.C. is not willing to give the general public some knowledge about its operations, then it can expect nothing but criticism for hiding behind a smokescreen of civil service bureaucracy, something which is not in the interests of the public. If the C.B.C. is not willing to give this information, then the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) should be prepared to come into this house and give good reason why the information cannot be made available.
Motions for Papers
I agree that in some cases it may not be proper to provide such information, but when someone does a piece of work in the news field-and obviously newspapermen are well suited to that field-we should have enough information to form a pretty good idea of whether or not we are getting value for our money for the work being done. I am violently opposed to the practice of the C.B.C. having a list of newspapermen and calling on each one in turn to present his viewpoint. This is not in the interests of good broadcasting and is one of the reasons why C.B.C. programming has reached the stage where I am receiving many letters objecting to its news coverage.
[DOT] (6:40 p.m.)
At present I am getting many letters objecting to the C.B.C.'s mediocre public affairs program, "Sunday", which obviously is not keeping up with its competition on the other channels. I am surprised when, every time we raise a matter about the C.B.C., there is this hue and cry that it is a sacred cow about which there cannot be any discussion. I think it would do the C.B.C. a lot of good if it were more frank with members of parliament and the public in general. They should pay some attention to suggestions and criticisms. No matter who we are as individuals we will not like everything they do. They might hire Mr. Saywell whom I may like and Mr. Ricker whom I may not like. If, however, we should think that both these gentlemen are unacceptable or that their work is mediocre, we should have some way to indicate our disapproval or, if we approve of them, our approval. I do not think we should be placed in the position of having power to make a decision in these matters, but I do think a great deal more information could be provided by the minister.
It is time we changed the system by which the C.B.C reports to the house through the minister. I believe the minister should have more authority as to what she can demand they produce and what cannot be demanded. I do not see much difference between the situation of the C.B.C. in the production of this type of correspondence, and that of the Canadian National Railways when they are asked to produce correspondence. Very often when an individual member has a request of this nature he takes it to the minister who, in very strong language I presume, refers it to the Canadian National Railways. The minister in turn receives a reply which he then gives in the house to the member who asked the

question. This is not what is being done with the C.B.C. It seems to me that this is one of the weaknesses we should try to strengthen.
I should like to see in C.B.C. television the vibrant influence it has always been in radio. This has not been accomplished. One reason is that we pay out too much money for mediocrity to the people we hire. If some of these accounts were produced the public might be in a position to judge whether or not we are paying too much for mediocrity. I think on the other hand we might be surprised also to learn how much we sometimes receive for a very limited payment. It might balance out. I am not suggesting it will be all one way or all the other. I believe that if more information is provided by the C.B.C. the people will be able to get closer to its operations. speechtext:
No. I am very pleased that that question has been asked. I am absolutely opposed to the C.B.C. becoming a department of government. I used the example of the Minister of Transport reporting on behalf of the Canadian National Railways, because I see a similarity between that operation of a crown corporation and the operation of the C.B.C. as a crown corporation. There is however a vast difference when a question is asked concerning the C.B.C. To my knowledge the minister has never been able to come back with an answer which provides any detail concerning her discussion with the C.B.C. management.
I believe there is correspondence in the possession of the C.B.C. which they do not wish to have presented. When there is a good reason for that position, I think it should be honoured. On the other hand there is much information members might ask questions

about, not as to the running of programs but as to how much money is paid for a certain type of program. I would presume that such information is available to ACTRA, and that everyone who participates in the programs, whether in the C.B.C. or in C.T.V., can ascertain the range of rates paid, while we as members of parliament when asking for this kind of information receive a blanket refusal.
I presume the government will talk out this motion, even if it takes two and a half hours, rather than have these particular documents relating to two individuals presented. I think the reason the question has been asked is so that the government can refuse and therefore discredit the operations of the C.B.C. I may be unfair in this, but I think these two particular men are incidental. They should not be. This is a reasonable request which should be conveyed to the C.B.C. by the minister who speaks for the C.B.C., with the suggestion that she sees no objection to these figures being presented and advising them that unless they have a damned good reason they should provide the information.

and we would have a very different type of operation in the C.B.C. than we now have. He has brought out a very important principle which we all must consider carefully. The "I's" were dotted and the "T's" were crossed as a result of the question posed to the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Stewart).
Motions for Papers
What are we to do about these emanations of parliament or, as someone perhaps more aptly called them, these creatures of parliament which refuse to answer questions or give information? I refer not only to the C.B.C. but also to the Civil Service Commission and the Unemployment Insurance Commission. The remarks I intend to make apply equally to the others.
These creatures of parliament as the hon. member for Timiskaming suggested, have almost become sacred cows whose activities cannot be questioned by members of this house. In fact any member who tries to do so is considered "far out" or naughty. These organizations have been very careful through their propaganda to make sure they do not fall under the control of parliament. They are financed by the taxpayers, but apparently no one outside those organizations has any control over them.
While I agree that there must be special limitations in control over these creations, and while I do not have time to go into that aspect of the matter, the situation now is that they are not responsible to the public and not responsible to this house. More and more of these creations are being established and I think hon. members ought to examine very carefully into whether these creatures should be allowed to go off on their own, without any de facto control.
Many people argue that there should not be any political influence in the C.B.C., so as to prevent its becoming a government mouthpiece. I think all hon. members will agree with that theory. We do not want political control and interference from within the C.B.C. itself. However, apparently this is what has happened, particularly in view of the extreme bias shown by this organization in reporting news items. Again I have not sufficient time to go into details and will reserve the right to do so on another occasion.
I suggest the same situation applies in respect of the Civil Service Commission. It has been said that we should not have political interference in the appointment of officials and that we do not want political patronage, but I am sure most hon. members will agree there are all sorts of devices used within the civil service for exactly that purpose. No one who has been around here for any length of time could be ignorant of the fact that there does exist a special kind of patronage within the commission. For example it is curious to find that very often qualifications set up to cover created positions fit to a remarkable
March 9, 1987

Equalization Payments to Provinces degree certain individuals lined up for those positions.
Hon. members must decide sooner or later the degree of control that should be exercised by the house over organizations which have become complete entities unto themselves. I agree there must be some limitation of parliamentary control, but the situation at the moment is highly unsatisfactory.
The hon. member for York-Humber is asking for some simple information which could not possibly prejudice the financial activities of the C.B.C. in competition with the C.T.V., but the corporation has refused to provide that information. I suggest there is no sound reason for such refusal and that the C.B.C. has refused because it is afraid of setting a precedent. This organization does not wish to give information on any subject.
I am reminded of a situation which existed when a former member for Temiscouata, now in the other place, used to ask a former president of the Canadian National Railways how much was being paid for charcoal and fence posts. The president of the railways used to turn purple in the face and tell the hon. member that it was none of his business. But that former member was very shrewd and somehow always managed to get the information.
Unfortunately few of the members of this house have had the opportunity in recent years of examining the spending estimates of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. For some reason or another they have always been brought forward at the end of our discussion on estimates, on the last day of a session or when the time has run out. We have not had the opportunity recently for any examination in the house of C.B.C expenditures. While this organization and its activities have been referred to in certain committees, the great majority of us have not had the opportunity of examining its operations. Whenever we ask questions about its activities, and why they will not give us certain information, we are told by the pipe line or the mouthpiece of that organization in the house, that the disclosure would not be in the public interest. We should like to know why this would not be in the public interest.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to say a few words on the measure before us I want first of all to assure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) that he should not be too quick to take too seriously all the things said by the Premier of Saskatchewan. I should also like to refer to the fact that the premier of our province has described the deal that he received at the hands of the Minister of Finance as a dirty deal, in so far as concerns the equalization that would come to my province.
In dealing with the situation with regard to the resource industries in a province I should like to point out that Saskatchewan at the present time is particularly interested in potash, the effects of this industry and the revenues derived therefrom. I believe this resource contributed in some degree to the decision taken by the minister in arriving at the formula, so far as concerns the phasing out of the equalization grants for Saskatchewan. While these industries are desirable for a province and increase the revenue of the country, they are not all gravy as far as the province and municipalities are concerned.
For this reason I wish the minister had taken into consideration the situation of the municipalities in this whole context when the government tried to arrive at a formula for the provinces. In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read part of an article which appeared in "The Rural Councillor", a municipal magazine in the province of Sas-

Fertile Belt, in which is located Esterhazy, the only large residential centre near the mines-

The other problem that has faced the provinces and municipalities is the critical lack of housing in potash mining areas in Saskatchewan. I wanted to bring that to the attention of the minister, because in light of the resource development which has taken place over the long-term period, when one considers the population of that province in relation to the bill now before us it would almost seem that the government has decided to discriminate against those provinces that are trying to develop the natural resources of our country. This is a very poor policy for the federal government of Canada to be following at a time when the high standard of living which Canadians expect demands a greater
development of our resources to sustain the increased costs that have to be met.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few remarks to make in connection with this bill. Similarly to other hon. members on this side of the house I cannot agree with the decision of the government to phase out the Technical and Vocational Training Assistance Act which was brought in by the Diefenbaker government, and with much success. I am sure it is generally recognized that the technical institutes built by the action of the former government filled a great need and provided an answer to the growing need for technical training to meet the present manpower requirements.
I have a particular interest in the future of technical institutes, the construction cost of which the former government paid from 50 to 75 per cent. There is a very fine technical institute in my city of Moose Jaw and it is filling a great need. It was officially opened by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) who at that time was the minister of labour. The government of which he was a minister paid 50 per cent of the construction costs, and because of the demand for technical training an addition was built, 75 per cent of the construction cost of which was covered by the federal government.
I mention these facts to emphasize the importance of the Moose Jaw technical institute and the need to expand the operations there. The Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh), as reported at page 13689 of Hansard, speaking
March 9, 1967

Equalization Payments to Provinces about federal help in post-secondary education adjustment payments, said:
The central concept In this plan is that the fiscal transfers will be calculated in relation to postsecondary operating expenditures only. The federal government considers this the only satisfactory measuring stick of rising education costs, and is prepared to increase its future transfers by the rate of increase in these costs. I must stress, however, that it is the province which determines upon the allocation of these funds, and it will have to do so in the light of both the operating and capital requirements of post-secondary institutions. The funds transferred are calculated in relation to operating expenditures, but are intended for use in both the operating and capital areas.
I want to emphasize the last part of the statement in which the Secretary of State said that the grants are intended for use in both the operating and capital areas.
I see a danger in handing the complete administration of these funds to the provincial government. With a provincial election coming in the very near future and with a $7 million grant in the next fiscal year I believe there is a danger that the provincial government may decide to use this federal grant for the purpose of building another technical institute in some other city. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on second reading of Bill No. C-277, I will not say much since the minister is well aware of what Quebec members think of the equalization payments and particularly of this act entitled:
An act to authorize the making of certain fiscal payments to provinces, to authorize the entry into tax collection agreements with provinces, and to amend the Established Programs (Interim Arrangements) Act.
What strikes me in all that, is the two words before last, "Interim Arrangements", because we are still hoping in Quebec that all those agreements, all the present arrangements, all those meetings with the provinces are of an interim nature only and that Quebec will one day win back what the constitution has guaranteed her since 1867, namely the recovery of her three taxation fields.
Of course, we cannot object now to the small share which is given us because we realize-and I want to point that out, here, to the minister-that the federal government is taking the lion's share and leaving to the provinces the hare's share. It has the cake and when it has taken its share, it remembers the provinces and gives them the crumbs. Every day we find that the federal government cuts largely into that cake, it makes fabulous and exorbitant expenses and even reaches the end of certain quarters with surpluses. And yet, it is always seeking new taxation fields.
This afternoon I listened to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) quote the amounts of equalization payments some provinces would receive. The minister
March 9, 1967

had said before that four provinces would not benefit from equalization because they were too rich. If I were a citizen of those provinces, there would be no advantage for me to commend the minister's words, although the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam suggested, without saying so specifically, that Quebec enjoys a special status by getting $235 million in equalization payments.
I suggest that what he forgot to mention, or what he did not want to mention, is that Quebec alone has as many people as the other five provinces together. When speaking of equalization, we should not compare Quebec with Newfoundland, Nova Scotia or New Brunswick. At this stage, I should like to call the attention of the house to the fact that the population of New Brunswick, Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and Manitoba are probably not much greater than that of the province of Quebec; these provinces will nevertheless receive a total of $215 million, whereas Quebec will get $235 million. One must not forget that although the province of Quebec will receive this amount, it has been taxed according to population, since taxes are always proportionate to population.
When all comes to all-this is why I said a while ago that we are only getting bits and pieces-when we look at the money the federal government takes out of the province of Quebec and the money returned, having picked up billions of dollars in this province,
I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that there is no reason to jump for joy. However, we could go on talking for hours on end and it would serve no purpose, since talking to the hon. member is like talking to solid rock: he merely smiles. I do not know whether he is laughing at us, or if he always sports such a wide smile. I am under the impression that our speeches are not being heard; however, we are waiting for the government of our province to take action, to demand what belongs to the province as a matter of right.
I should like to state here, in this house, that if the Quebec government wants more autonomy, it must make the first move. It should not wait until Ottawa takes action because every time this happened, Ottawa took advantage of the opportunity to penetrate more deeply into our fields of taxation. It is therefore up to the hon. premier of the province of Quebec, it is up to the Quebec government to make a stand, to demand that the federal government respect its rights and put a stop to this procrastinating. We want him to mind his business here and let

Equalization Payments to Provinces us collect our taxes in the province. We are old enough to collect our taxes. It seems to me we would be relieving him of this great burden resting on his shoulders. He says himself it is a tremendous burden and we want to relieve him of it. Let him simply give us the right devolved upon us by the constitution to collect our taxes and we shall administer our own affairs with our taxes.
This year, 75 per cent of succession duties will be returned to the provinces. As for personal and corporate income taxes, I hope that the minister will at least add a certain percentage each year, so that in two or three years, all succession duties and all personal and corporate income taxes will be returned to the provinces. I feel that the federal government and the hon. minister would avoid a big headache if they put a stop to this practice which consists in levying taxes in provinces and then returning their money by means of various payments. The minister says that he is returning the product of the tax to the province. Well, if he is returning the product of the tax, why go to all the trouble of taxing the province in the first place? Why not leave these taxes to the provinces? We simply want to lighten the burden of the hon. Minister of Finance.
If the other provinces want to do otherwise, they are free to do so, but if we want to relieve the federal government a little, if we want to reduce its work and, especially, alleviate the burden of this double administration, often the cause of financial troubles and misunderstandings on the administrative level, I do not see why the government does not accept our suggestion.

Many a misunderstanding would be done away with if, once and for all, the matter were settled. If the federal government wants to pay 50, 75 or even 80 per cent of those courses, it should pay the amount to the provinces and let them implement those

administration today can determine or establish a clear and definite dividing line between the powers of each of the three levels of government, federal, provincial and municipal.
And I should like to have it remembered, throughout the remarks I shall make as briefly as possible, that I recognize the principle that the municipalities are legal creatures of the provincial governments. By leave, I should like to come back in a few minutes to some remarks made in respect of the tax distribution at the three

Though still largely overlooked as a serious subject for study, municipal governments are now carrying some of the most critical responsibilities for public policy. The quality and efficiency of our urban communities where more than 70 per cent of Canadians now live-

-and where 80 per cent or more will live by 1980, depend to a large extent on decisions made by municipal authorities and on the financial and technical assistance received by them from senior governments.

And if I mention it, Mr. Speaker, and I will mention another with your permission, it is precisely because I will repeat what I said earlier: in all those federal-provincial talks, everyone seems to forget that there is a third level of government which, in the opinion of many well-informed people, is just as important as the others, although it has less prestige, because it is closer to the people and has to face problems which are more vital, more essential in some respects than the others, although I know very well that the three levels of government must work hand in hand. Mr. Speaker, this is proved by the figures presented in this brief. I see here that the general administrative expenses of the municipalities, in all the provinces of Canada-

And what were the revenues, Mr. Speaker? It is simple. In 1933, when the municipalities were spending $303 million, their revenues totalled $294 million. Therefore, they had a deficit. Mr. Speaker, that is precisely what I am driving at. What I want to say here is that, in all these discussions, all these conversations, all these negotiations between the federal and provincial governments, the municipalities are treated like abnormal orphans, like poor children who must be content with the mouthful of bread they are condescendingly given. What is more, they are expected not to be too demanding, as they are not even allowed to participate in the round table dialogues, as they should, in view of their considerable responsibilities toward the taxpayers. Their responsibilities may perhaps even be greater than those of the other governments, may be even more critical, because they live from day to day with the citizens, hear their complaints every day, and must find solutions to those problems, while

often having their hands and feet bound by the superior administrations.
If the Fathers of Confederation came back to earth, they would be amazed at how things they knew have changed in 100 years. And they would find it difficult to understand how one can take the liberty of dealing so lightly with the officials of that third level of government known as municipal authorities.
I say that mayors and aldermen are martyrs of the public cause, for they are the ones who hear the repercussions of what is done in the House of Commons and in the provincial legislatures, as the electors do not often have an opportunity of seeing their M.P. or M.L.A. and complain to their aider-men and mayor. And very often they do not understand why municipal administrations do not have the powers they should, why they do not have the finance required to meet the needs of the municipality.
Mr. Speaker, the mayors have been asking for several years to be allowed to participate in the federal-provincial conferences. This request has been made through the Canadian Federation of Mayors, comprising all municipalities in every province. Together, they try to examine the problems of municipalities in the light of the experience of mayors and aldermen of the most important municipalities of the country, with the help of the best economists, the best statisticians, the advice of the most reputable sociologists invited to attend their convention. The members of the federation make this request even if they were only allowed to sit in as observers-the municipalities realize that they are merely provincial bodies-in order to see how their fate is discussed and in order to put forth, occasionally, constructive and intelligent suggestions in order to help certain ministers or premiers upon whose decisions depends the fate of municipalities. These decisions are often the result of haphazard consideration and are often made by people who are not familiar with municipal government.
Some provinces-and I know, because I have toured the ten provinces several times and on many instances I have met municipal heads and administrators-have reduced the role of municipal administration to the so-called rubber stamp, and they are not even given that basic privilege of being asked for their advice about legislation on municipal affairs.
I glanced over the Carter report-of course, I did not have time to read all those things-
March 9, 1987	COMMONS
but I went over it with a curiosity that you will understand after what I have just told you, in order to try and find what could be said in it about the implications of those recommendations on municipal administration.
In my opinion, the Carter report, is a masterpiece, it contains recommendations which are absolutely valid, which will certainly involve a fiscal revolution and will probably create an economic climate that will indirectly assist the municipalities.
But I would have liked to see in that, as in some other documents coming from the provinces of Canada, an awareness that the municipal governments, exist, that they are grouped, provincially, in a union of municipalities and federally grouped in the Canadian federation of mayors, that they are entitled to have a say in the matter and that, in most cases, they have in this third level administration an experience greater than that of most of those who are legislating on a higher level.
Mr. Speaker, to show that I am not imagining such things, I wish to point out that even if the municipalities are provincial creatures, there are, nevertheless, joint fields of authority and of responsibility where the three levels of government must step in.
I should like to enumerate a few, very briefly, and without comments. The three levels of government are trying, of course, to improve the living conditions of their constituents. The elected representatives at the municipal level see their constituents and hear their representations night and a day.
Those who among my colleagues have been mayors or councillors know that it is not unheard of to be awakened in the middle of the night by people reminding them that they are unemployed, that they cannot take advantage of this or that piece of social legislation, that the entrance to their house or yard has not been cleared. They know that is part of the social awareness that the municipal administrator must keep alive twenty-four hours a day.
There is the winter works program which should be financed by the federal government and which, in my opinion, should be amended somewhat, brought up to date to take into account the present situation. There is the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, there is urban renewal which is a tragic problem in a great number of municipalities. There 23033-873

There is also unemployment which is precisely the great plague of municipal authorities, because if the federal and the provincial governments fail to take appropriate action to alleviate unemployment, mayors and aldermen are the ones who listen day in and day out to the grievances of the jobless. Taxes of all kinds drain the financial resources of the taxpayers to such an extent that municipal authorities are unable to draw up their budgets.
Mr. Speaker, I could refer to many other things, but I do not want to overtax the patience of the house. In conclusion, I have a simple and practical suggestion to offer the Minister of Finance. I see he is busy with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Pepin) and I am not blaming him, because it is always wise to draw near to wealth, whether natural or artificial, but to make sure that the minister understands me-I am aware of his worthy efforts to learn French and I would not want him to be vexed at my procedure but rather to consider it as an effort at understanding on my part-I shall try to make my point in a language which is not my own-
[DOT] (9:00 p.m.)

There are three levels of government in this country, the federal, the provincial and the municipal. Each has its own responsibilities and each must have the means to carry out its responsibilities. I think one thing is missing; that is, municipal governments are not consulted often enough. For years and years they have been asking that they be allowed to attend these conferences between the federal and provincial governments so that they would know what is going on, and so that they would have an opportunity eventually to speak their minds, since they have a very heavy responsibility. I would suggest that we establish in this country the type of intergovernmental advisory commission they have in the United States, which operates for 12 months of the year and which is assisted by a task force-and this is a word I heard this afternoon-of specialized people. This intergovernmental advisory commission, board or whatever you might call it, would be made

Equalization Payments to Provinces up of representatives of the federal government, the provinces, and the municipal governments which have their own organization, the Canadian Federation of Mayors.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to insist on this. Most of the time when one speaks of municipalities he is not taken seriously. In the minds of many people these governments are considered secondary, because after all they are composed of mayors and aldermen. The prime ministers and ministers of the provinces control them and sometimes have them elected or defeated. However, they have their responsibilities, and need the financial means to exercise those responsibilities. I think we should bear this in mind when we discuss financial arrangements between federal and provincial governments, because the province is supposed to be the father of the municipalities which, I am sorry to say, is not always so.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to delay unduly the second reading of this very important bill. There are, however, one or two principles in it with which I must disagree, and I take this opportunity to make known my disagreement. I am convinced that the proposal in the bill to relate equalization payments to the average of all the provinces of Canada very definitely is a backward step and one which will react unfavourably on the poorer provinces of Canada. I refer particularly to my own province of Prince Edward Island.
At this time I should like to place before the house, before the government and the minister just as succinctly and concisely as I can the situation in which the province of Prince Edward Island finds itself at the present time, in so far as being able to finance its essential services is concerned. I think probably I can exemplify this very clearly first of all by pointing out the debt situation in which Prince Edward Island, the smallest province of Canada, finds itself.
I should like to go back over a three year period, starting March 31, 1963. The direct debt of this province at that time, less of course our sinking funds, was $38,709,000, or $362 per capita. One year later, March 31, 1964, the direct debt had increased from $38,709,000 to $50,059,000, or $468 per capita. As of March 31, 1965, the net direct debt had increased again from $50,059,000 to $56,200,000, or $520 per capita. Finally, as of March 31, 1966, the last fiscal year for which definite
March 9, 1967	COMMONS
figures are available, that debt had increased from $56,200,000 to $62,200,000 or $575 per capita. That, Mr. Speaker, represents an increase in debt for a small province of only 108,000 people over a three-year period of 62 per cent.
For the year ending March 31, 1967-the end of this present fiscal year-it is estimated it will take $4,300,000 to service this debt. This amount of $4,300,000 must come out of our revenues. It is required to pay the interest on what we owe and to establish an adequate sinking fund to meet our provincial debentures when they fall due. I should like to point out that under the proposed agreement in respect of this bill which is before us now our province will receive from the federal government under this arrangement a total of $14 million. It will take 30 per cent of that $14 million simply to pay the interest on and service the present debt.
From these figures I believe it must be obvious that that $14 million certainly will not be enough. If we look at it from another angle, our revenue from provincial sources for the year ending March 31, 1967-this is the revenue we will collect from our own taxpayers-will amount to only $12,500,000. That is the amount our government can collect from its taxpayers. Out of that $12,500,000 we first must take $4,300,000 and set it aside to service our debt. In other words 35 per cent of our provincial revenue must go immediately to service the provincial debt, pay the interest and provide an adequate sinking fund.
[DOT] (9:10 p.m.)
It is obvious to anyone who takes a close look at the figures that our province is heavily dependent upon the revenues we hope to receive from Ottawa. Our total estimated revenue to March 31, 1967, is $33,500,000. That is the total amount our government has available to it to run the province, and of that $33,500,000 we will receive $21 million from Ottawa. In other words, 60 per cent of our total revenue will come from Ottawa. Ours is the only province in Canada that receives more from Ottawa than it collects from its own taxpayers. I am only pointing this out to impress upon this government just how heavily a province such as ours is dependent on the federal treasury.
I submit very seriously that we in the province of Prince Edward Island cannot pay more in taxes. That is because our tax potential is extremely low. We have the lowest wage earners in Canada. The average weekly 23033-8731
Equalization Payments to Provinces wage in our province is $64 as compared to the Canadian average of $96.53. Our wage earners receive about $32.50 below the national average.
According to the latest figures available the average Canadian makes $5,000 per year. In Prince Edward Island the average is $3,600 per year. We have greater unemployment and underemployment than any other province in Canada. In December of 1966, we see that 5.8 per cent of the labour force in the Atlantic provinces was unemployed, as compared with only 2.4 per cent in Ontario. Taking into account the very low per capita income, I very seriously suggest we do not have the tax potential in our province to provide through our own revenues the essential services to which people are justly entitled.
One might very well ask what are the causes of this low per capita income. I suggest there are several, including the loss of our markets to the south, the increase in tariff barriers against our exports, the opening up of supplies of natural products from other countries and the centralization of industries in close proximity to big population centres. We find it extremely difficult to encourage industry to come to our province. Our geographical isolation is probably another reason our per capita income is so low.
Often we talk about the war on poverty. I suggest that one of the most effective weapons with which successfully to fight this war is a plan whereby we can bring about a more equal distribution of our national wealth. If a plan could be devised to bring about a more equal distribution, then we in our province would benefit and our people would be able to contribute more to the provincial treasury by way of taxes.
National prosperity is not spread equally throughout the provinces and regions of this country, and regional disparities in incomes and opportunities have persisted. I suggest they will continue to persist until we hit upon a more socially equitable policy for distributing income throughout the economy.
For the past 100 years our biggest export from Prince Edward Island has been in the form of brains. Statistics conclusively indicate that our birth rate over the years has far exceeded our death rate, but our population remains at about the 100,000 mark. It has stayed at that point for 50, 75 or 100 years.
You may well ask what has happened to our natural increase. It is syphoned off to other parts of Canada, where the prospects
13814	COMMONS
Equalization Payments to Provinces and opportunities of enjoying a higher standard of living are greater than in our own province. I suggest therefore that until such time as effective measures can be devised to bring our incomes at least close to the national average, we must lean heavily on Ottawa in order that we may enjoy the same measure of essential services being enjoyed by other provinces of Canada. Of course as fellow Canadians and citizens of this great country we are entitled to the enjoyment of the same essential services as are enjoyed by the other provinces, in spite of the fact our unfortunate position is such that we cannot possibly provide these from our own revenue. It must not be forgotten that we are citizen of Canada, and that it is not through any fault of ours our incomes are not high enough to provide sufficient tax to enable our government to give us these services.
Any fiscal policy inaugurated between the federal and provincial governments must take into consideration the fiscal ability of a province to maintain a national standard of service. This is the area in which this proposed arrangement falls down drastically. It does not take into consideration the fiscal ability of the province to provide essential services.
Every Canadian from Newfoundland to British Columbia expects, quite rightly, the same quality of services in education, highways, health and welfare, transportation and in other well established government programs. That is all we ask. We do not want to be considered as poor relations in this great confederacy, nor do we ask for any privileges. We do not want any; but we do very vigorously claim a recognition of a right to fiscal equality. We shall never be satisfied until that right is afforded us.
As I mentioned before, ours is one of the provinces with inadequate tax collection potentials and we must have a substantial increase over and above the amount we are to receive under this proposed bill. The provisions of this measure definitely do not go far enough to meet our needs. No arrangement will be satisfactory which does not make it financially possible for our province to provide a reasonable level of provincial services without imposing an abnormal burden of tax, because our people cannot bear that burden of taxation. This is the basic and indispensable minimum requirement of any division of revenues between the heads of government and the measure of relief given to us under the provisions of this bill. An additional $3,500,000 does not come anywhere near meeting this requirement
[Mr. McQuaid.l

We take the position in our province that federal-provincial agreements must seek to attain a balance between the financial capacity and the responsibilities of government, and we therefore must have a formula based on fiscal need.
[DOT] (9:20 p.m.)
Fiscal need is the only satisfactory base upon which any formula can be devised. The policy which is incorporated in this bill, that of relating equalization payments to the average per capita revenue of all the provinces of Canada, is very definitely not in accord with the principle of fiscal need and is not satisfactory to us.
Another thing we are disappointed about is that the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants-those grants which have meant so much to us in past years-while strictly speaking they are not being abolished, they are losing their identity. I suggest it is not fair to have the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants incorporated in our equalization grants. I am afraid that this is only the thin edge of the wedge. The Atlantic provinces adjustment grants as such will be no more. I realize that the 3i million we have been receiving each year under the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants is now being incorporated in the $14 million we are about to receive, but it goes in under the heading of equalization. I do not think this is right. I think the identity of the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants should have been maintained.
I would suggest three remedial measures that will give us and the other poorer provinces of Canada the relief which we need, the relief to which as a province of this country we are entitled. The first would be a basic payment across the board to those provinces with a low fiscal capacity and a low tax potential. This refers to any province that has a low fiscal capacity-that is, the earning power of its people is not sufficient to allow them to pay taxes to provide the essential services that are required-and a low tax potential. With regard to the provinces which find themselves in this situation, I very seriously suggest that they should first of all receive a basic payment. Second, I suggest that the present equalization payments must be averaged to the highest income province in Canada, and not to the national average. These equalization payments should not be geared to the national average of all the provinces of Canada but rather to the revenue of the highest income province. Third, Mr. March 9, 1967
Speaker, I suggest an increase in the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants from the present $35 million to $60 million a year.
These suggested amendments would certainly result in an improvement in the financial arrangements suggested in the present bill and would help our province and other provinces which find themselves in practically the same situation to meet the mounting costs of provincial services, without resorting to an abnormal burden of taxation. I suggest that as a province of Canada this is the minimum to which we are entitled. I very seriously recommend these three remedial measures to the minister before we pass the present bill.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I listened with interest this evening to the minister's preliminary statement. As usual it was a very reasoned one and one that I know will strike some response in my own province of British Columbia, because we are a province of very reasonable people.

At the same time, Mr. Speaker, I must confess that we are one of the "have" provinces. Any time a British Columbian begins to talk about his own province it becomes immediately obvious that ours is one of the provinces of this great country that has been particularly blessed. Therefore there is a danger inherent in the sort of lengthy and seemingly complete bill before us this evening, when it is considered with the reasoned statement of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp), that too reasonable people will think our province has really nothing further to ask of any federal government. But I would submit, Mr. Speaker, that this is a delusion.
It is one of our Canadian problems, that too many of the schemes, proposals and arrangements that are put forward for the development of this country become rescue operations, rather than operations designed to assist the provinces that are in a position to go ahead. We in British Columbia feel that there are many areas in which our province has not had the kind of assistance from the federal government that has been given to other provinces. This problem is sometimes concerned with geography.
I might mention that although we are very proud of our history and the fact that Vancouver Island and the mainland formed a political union a long time ago, we realize
Equalization Payments to Provinces now it was fiscal folly to do so in the light of what has happened to date. Had our people had sufficient foresight into the development of this country, they would never have united Vancouver Island and the mainland; they would have left Vancouver Island as an individual province. If that had been done, the city of Vancouver would now have no problems in connecting its heart with the north shore, because the federal government would have seen that highways were built; and there would be a project at least under way, if not completed, to build a bridge, causeway or tunnel between the mainland and Vancouver Island. We can see now, with hindsight, that perhaps what seemed such a farsighted view 100 years ago was really something that eventually posed a problem.
In this connection, Mr. Speaker, I would mention our railroad, the Pacific Great Eastern, which because it is a provincially owned railroad has never been on the same sort of financial footing as other railroads in this country. I might tell the house a story about that railroad. I lived in the little village of Lillooet, in the Fraser canyon, for several years and the Pacific Great Eastern Railway ran through that village. We had a very good friend, an immigrant from Germany, who lived in the house beside ours. She did not know the history of British Columbia very well. Her house, like ours, overlooked the railway track, and she watched trains go by every day of the year, month after month. One evening she came over to us, much agitated because something strange had happened that afternoon; A train had gone by and the whole village had risen as one and rushed to the bank overlooking the railway track to watch it pass.
Our neighbour could not understand why this had happened. I explained that it was really very simple. There had been a disastrous series of slides in the Fraser canyon which had completely blocked off the two major railways, the C.P.R. and the C.N.R., from the city of Vancouver, and for the first time in history the Canadian National had run a train over the tracks of the Pacific Great Eastern down to Vancouver, in order to bring freight in, while they were waiting for repairs to be carried out. The little village of Lillooet appreciated the fact that for the first time there had been forced upon that other great railroad recognition of the fact that the Pacific Great Eastern actually existed. out to that province, or have gone home to it and informed the people of British Columbia that large sums of money are waiting in some federal treasury if only the provincial government would ask for them. We have heard this repeatedly. They talk about these funds when there is either a federal or provincial election, and this story has been so common and so current in British Columbia for several years now that it is not surprising that the premier of British Columbia, who is also a reasonable man, has reached the point of sending a telegram to the Minister of Finance asking whether it would be possible to borrow $100 million from the federal government to be used for the development of hydro schemes on the Peace and Columbia rivers. These hydro schemes were about to be undertaken when the federal government increased the sales tax on construction materials to 11 per cent. This measure which affected construction in all provinces in Canada and was perhaps the most inflationary measure brought in by any Canadian government was one that affected particularly British Columbia.
The premier of British Columbia is a reasonable man and I am sure he knew that $100 million would not be forthcoming as rapidly as some people thought it would, but it was one way of solving the nagging question which I have been asked many times myself and that is: "How about these large sums of federal money? What is wrong with the government of British Columbia that it does not go ahead and ask for some of this money? We are told that it is there, why is the request not made?" The request has been made. An hon. member says that it was made so long ago that even the interest on that sum would amount to a considerable sum of money, and I would agree with that.
I have read the statement made by the minister on March 2 in which he referred to this request. Unfortunately I was not present in the house at the time. I am glad to hear that the statement was much more reasonable than the answers which he gave in the house to questions put to him by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I know how concerned that hon. member is over this whole question, and I know of the high regard in which he holds the policies that are carried out by the government of British Columbia.
I do not intend to oppose this bill because I believe that it does improve the situation in British Columbia in several respects. However, I would like to make it very clear that it does not solve a host of problems in British
