Columbia, simply because our province attracts people from many other areas in Canada. For example many problems arise in providing hospitals for the aged. In this connection we hope that some day the federal government will be able to increase its per capita grants for hospital construction, an increase that has been long awaited and long overdue in our province.
We also have problems in providing education, because of the families which have moved to our province as a result of its booming economy. I would remind hon. members from other provinces in Canada, whose population is more static and who speak about the brain drain, that they can congratulate themselves on the fact that at least they can cope with the educational problems their provinces have, because in British Columbia it is very difficult indeed to cope with all the demands of education at the present time. I know that this bill will improve somewhat the situation in post-secondary education, but I am concerned about the problems that will arise.
There is a great need for some sort of a federal bureau of education in order to discuss carefully what federal policy will mean in terms of actual schools in the province, to which this legislation will be applied, because it does not take much change in the grants policy to distort the educational picture in a province and to influence the structure of its educational system. Confusion can arise over what is meant by junior matriculation, in view of the fact that some provinces require three years of secondary education before junior matriculation, while others have four years. The whole system of secondary education may well be adjusted in some provinces in order to enable them to benefit to the greatest extent possible from the federal grant.
Finally I would like to say a word about the vexing problem of estate taxes, which has been mentioned already in this debate. The Carter commission had some important things to say about estate taxes. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) was concerned about the fact that there was a five year time limit on this bill. He was afraid that the Carter commission report would run into interference from this bill. I do not think he needs to worry about this because I suspect many more than five years will have
Equalization Payments to Provinces passed before any of the major recommendations of the Carter commission are implemented, judging by the present pace of legislation and the progress which we experience in this parliament.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I hope that the government will move to amend the estate tax requirements and not await any general implementation of the Carter commission report. Because I think the time has gone by when businesses in Canada can afford to be disrupted upon the death of the owner. Sometimes deaths are premature and unexpected, and far too often businesses either have to be sold or undergo a complete change of management in order that estate taxes may be paid.
I am sure that any member who sat on the drug costs committee, Mr. Speaker, heard repeated over and over again the story of drug companies which used to be Canadian, but because their owners were getting on in years and no member of the family wished to take over the company and face the prospect of meeting enormous bills for estate taxes, it became necessary to sell these companies. Because of the size of some of the companies the United States was the only place that could put up the capital, and as a result many of the companies appearing before the committee were wholly-owned United States subsidiaries, instead of being Canadian-owned.
Why is this, Mr. Speaker? Books have been written suggesting that the cause of this is United States economic imperialism; but I contend that far too often the cause has been the tax policies of the government of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR FEDERAL PAYMENTS TO PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, from 1933 until 1956 there was a provincial Liberal government in my native province. From 1935 until 1957 there was a federal Liberal government in Ottawa. During the whole of this period efforts were made by the various Liberal premiers who held office in Halifax to secure recognition by the Liberal government in Ottawa of the very obvious plight of the maritime provinces. Far too often the late and great Angus L. Macdonald came to Ottawa looking for assistance, and went home empty handed. His successor, Henry Hicks, had the same fate in store. If the Liberal government had not been defeated in the general election campaign in 1957 I dare say that Robert Stanfield would have enjoyed no greater success than his predecessors.

March 9. 1967
Equalization Payments to Provinces
However, Mr. Speaker, in 1957 the Dief-enbaker administration was elected to office and almost immediately the Atlantic provinces found a government with a national policy as well as a regional policy that recognized the special problems of the Atlantic provinces and tried to do something about them.
When I same to this house in 1957 I was impressed indeed by the work of the late George C. Nowlan, who at that time as minister of national revenue put forward the special problems facing the Atlantic provinces and secured early in 1958 the passage of legislation which provided through the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants the sum of $25 million a year for those Atlantic provinces. This was special recognition, Mr. Speaker. The total sum provided at the time was $100 million spread over a four year period.
As the four year period drew to an end, the Diefenbaker administration did not say to the Atlantic provinces: "Well, you have gotten $100 million more than expected when we were elected to office; we do not feel that you should have more, even though your problems continue to exist and persist". Instead, Mr. Speaker, the Diefenbaker administration passed further legislation in 1962 continuing the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants for a further five year period, and increasing from $25 million to $35 million the yearly amount paid.
We are today debating legislation that will eliminate the special recognition granted to the Atlantic provinces by the Diefenbaker administration. To this I object as strenuously as I can, Mr. Speaker. I ignore and discount the argument that is put forward that it is all going into the pot; that it is going to be part of the scheme of things in the future. What the government is doing now, in effect, is eliminating this special recognition that was afforded to the Atlantic area when the Conservative government took office in 1958, and passed this legislation.
Surely there is money available for the present through the negotiations which have taken place; but this special recognition that was made is no longer acknowledged, and the next time agreements are reached between the federal and provincial governments no thought will be given by the present administration, if it is lucky enough to still be in office at the time, to giving the Atlantic provinces the special recognition they deserve.

There is no difference between the problems we face today, Mr. Speaker, and the problems we faced in 1958 when this legislation was passed, except that probably the problems are not as great as they were as a result of the passage of this legislation. But the problems are there. We still have a higher rate of unemployment than any other part of the nation and a lower per capita income than any other part of the nation. As the hon. member for Kings (Mr. McQuaid) so ably pointed out in his address, the problems we had at confederation not only still exist but indeed have increased many, manyfold, the most significant increase occurring when a Liberal administration holds office in Ottawa. As far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, in the maritimes Liberal times are hard times.
The Progressive Conservative party have always urged special recognition of the Atlantic provinces in order to eliminate the disparity existing between that area and the rest of Canada. The Liberal party has continually ignored our problems and endeavoured to treat us in the same manner as any other part of the nation. When Liberal spokesmen go down to that area of Canada they recognize our special problems, but only for the period of time they spend there. As soon as they leave the Atlantic provinces the problems which are in their minds also seem to disappear. It will be a sad day for the Atlantic provinces when the Atlantic provinces adjustment grants go out the window, as they will on passage of this legislation.
The same thing happened to the Atlantic Development Board, Mr. Speaker. Our concept was that the Atlantic Development Board would endeavour to lift up the Atlantic provinces and assist the people there to lift themselves up. As soon as the Liberal party took office, we found the board downgraded. It was no longer the instrument through which we were to go forward, with hundreds of millions of dollars being poured into our area in the hope that the disparity could be eliminated. Instead, we found the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) telling us that the board was for the future. He even put a date on the future of the board, until we forced him to eliminate it. The position of the board in the future would be that of a gap filler, and indeed that has been its position.

No, I do not have the time. I will say this, that the board has effectively done the job this government gave to it, within the confines of the funds made available to it. However, it has not been the kind of board the Progressive Conservative party envisaged when they established it. It has not done the kind of job that we had hoped such a board would do. The sad fact of the matter is that this government seems determined to eliminate from the statute books of this nation any legislation specifically directed toward eliminating the disparities and recognizing the problems facing the Atlantic provinces.
This is the thing that I abhor the most, the fact that this government is unwilling to recognize our specific problems, is unwilling to give us an opportunity to do the things in our part of Canada that will allow us to move forward with the remainder of this nation. Certainly if this legislation is passed in its present form, all the great work that the late George Nowlan did to see that the Atlantic provinces received special recognition is going to go out the window. Unfortunately there is little hope that this will not happen.
One need only look at the difficulties being experienced in the Cape Breton area of my province of Nova Scotia to realize that we have special problems. We are willing to face these problems, and attack them as best we can within the financial resources available to us. However, we do not have the finances to do so, and we do not get much help from this government. We have not received much help during the four years this government has held office. I do not know what the fate of the Atlantic provinces will be in the future if this government persists in eliminating all the good things that were done by the Diefen-baker administration.
I do not know whether this government realizes or cares to realize how serious these problems continue to be. We hear all kinds of excuses made about why this or that has not been done. We do not get the kind of action we deserve, and we do not get the kind of recognition that we need if we are going to close the gap, which is becoming an ever-widening gap between the Atlantic provinces and the rest of Canada. There does not appear to be any legislation on the order paper, or any prospects of legislation, with the exception of the special corporation which is to be set up to deal with the problems of the coal mining industry in Nova Scotia, that is going to help us eliminate the problems that are very much in evidence in our area.
Equalization Payments to Provinces
Surely to goodness, the government does not think the Cape Breton corporation, which is to eliminate the coal mining problem, in itself will meet all the problems of the Atlantic provinces. I know that in Cumberland county, as well as many other counties, there is ample evidence to indicate a great deal more must be done. Surely, there is not much evidence for the people of the Atlantic provinces to indicate that anything more will be done, if this government continues to move forward as slowly as it has up to now.
We in the Atlantic provinces are told many wonderful stories at election time, and have been told those stories during the last 100 years. Until the Diefenbaker government was elected in 1957, these were nothing more than stories. They were just pie in the sky. But the pie disappeared the day after the votes were counted. During the seven years the Diefenbaker government held office we got action; we got results and we got legislation.

ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE-APPOINTMENT OP UNILINGUAL LIAISON OFFICER WITH EXPO '67
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon, on the orders of the day, I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Pennell) if it were true that a unilingual R.C.M.P. inspector had been appointed liaison officer between the federal police and the security service at Expo and, if so, if the minister would take steps to appoint a bilingual officer to that important post.
I felt prompted to ask that question after reading in the Montreal newspaper La Presse on Wednesday, March 8, a news report that read as follows:
An inspector of the R.C.M.P., unable to speak a single word of French, has been appointed liaison officer between the federal police and the security service of Expo.
Mr. J. A. B. Ryddel, who holds the rank of inspector, was stationed in New Brunswick until his recent appointment to Expo, an appointment which does not seem to please a number of members of the security force of Man and his World.
In the meetings all proceedings are carried out in French only. As Inspector Ryddel does not understand a single word of our language, the higher-ups of the R.C.M.P. had to delegate to him an interpreter who translates for him the words of the security officers.
Mr. Herve T. Poudrette, who heads the security services at Expo confirmed to La Presse that inspector Ryddel spoke only English but he refused to comment on the situation.

A spokesman for the R.C.M.P. at Montreal headquarters also confirmed that Inspector Ryddel spoke only one language but he also refused to comment.
On the other hand, an Expo official said: you would swear Commissioner G. B. McClellan of the R.C.M.P. tried on purpose to offend French Canadians by sending us this unilingual official.
Mr. Speaker, it is inconceivable that, $6 or $7 million having been spent on the Laur-endeau-Dunton commission on bilingualism and biculturalism, a man who does not speak French should be appointed to an important position in the city of Montreal.
In order to understand or to make himself understood, he needs an interpreter, and the dangers of that are quite clear.
Again, we realize that the commissioner of the R.C.M.P. is not working toward Canadian unity, and his gesture tends to sabotage all efforts toward national unity and peace in Canada.
The Solicitor General of Canada should remove Commissioner McClellan from his post for reasons of incompetence, and also replace by a bilingual official the R.C.M.P. inspector responsible for liaison between the various security bodies of Expo.

On behalf of the Solicitor General I should like to answer the question asked by the hon. member. May I first express my regret that I am unable to give this answer in the other language. With the increase in duties which the force will have to carry out during Expo it has been found necessary to increase, at least for this year, the number of commissioned officers stationed at Montreal to deal with matters arising, not only out of Expo but also from the general increase of federal police work anticipated during that period.
Every commissioned officer stationed in the province of Quebec, until the transfer of this officer, was bilingual. Inspector Riddell, who was a newly commissioned officer, was sent to Montreal for a two-fold purpose; not particularly as a liaison officer with Expo, nor was he designated as such. Rather, he was sent as a general officer in the division to be available for general duties wherever he may be required and where pressure demands extra help. The second purpose of the transfer was in line with the commissioner's endeavour to encourage the study of French by English speaking officers.
March 9, 1967	COMMONS
